MOSCOW, Aug. II. PraVda,
Communist Party newspaper, said
today a document has been found
in Seoul showing the South
Korean government planned germ
warfare against North Korea this
year.


Pravda said it was clear the
whole plan was American-inspired
and added that when top South
Korean intelligence agents are
caught. they will tell what
Americans gave the orders"


The paper said it was not clear
whether the necessary bacteria
were to come from warehouses at
Camp Dietrich. Germany, or from
Japan. Both areas are now under
American control.


The Soviet Union sentenced II
japanese Army officers to prison
terms ranging up to Is years last
December for allegedly plotting
germ warfare during World War
II. The government newspaper
Izvestia said then the trial was "a
blow at Anglo-American imperial
lists"


Radio Moscow said July 2 that
the United States had brought 18
other Japanese experts to Amer
lea to help plan meteorological
warfare.


Pravda's reference to Camp Diet
rich. Germany. apparently was a
mistaken reference to Camp Diet
rich. Md, which is the seat of the
Army's archaeological warfare re-
search.

TOKYO, Sunday, Sept. To-
The Korean Communists today
applied new pressure on the
northern front where American
and South Korean forces yester-
day closed a five-mile gap opened
by Red tanks.


Despite the pressure the north.
ern front defending the strategic
base of Taegu was described as
relatively quiet" by Associated
Press Correspondent Left Erick-
son at United States Eighth Army
headquarters.


Some of the Red heat on Taegu
was cooled by the closing of the
breach in the line between Yong
chon and Kyongju east of Taegu.
But the Reds still were a con-
tlnulng threat to the South Ko-
rean provisional capital from the
north. Powerful forces there have
been hammering incessantly at
American ridge positions seven
miles above Taegu. The Red Ko-
keans have massed $4,000 men
for new major drive against that
important Allied base.


Reds Win Battle Mountain.


In another main action yester-
day flercely attacking Communists
paid dearly in lives and won Bat
tie Mountain at the southern end
of the line, two miles from fire.
Quilted Haman and 81 air miles
west of the main supply port of
Pusan.


The Allied Air Force swarmed
back to the battlefront at dawn
today with only a medium over
cast to hinder the harassment Of
Red troops and supply lines.


The general quiet that had
fallen over the entire Korean bat
tleground since yesterdays blazing
actions on the north and south
was reflected in the absence Of
headquarters summaries. Both
Gen. MacArthur's and 9th Army
headquarters skipped their Sat-
urday night and Sunday morning
announcements.


The gap in the United Nations
northern defense wall was
snapped shut by South Korean
troops driving east from ongchon
and American and South Korean
forces moving west from Kyongju.
Communist tank columns had
opened the hole earlier in the
week.


Yongchon, gateway city to
Taegu 20 miles westward, was re-
captured by South Koreans Fri
day from the armor-led Reds who
had held it briefly. The ousted
Reds poured artillery and mortar
fire on the city. The North Ko-
rean radio has claimed possession
of Yongchon for two days.


Several groups of Reds were
pocketed by the forces that closed
the Yongchon-Kyongju opening.


Situation Much Improved


A United States Army spokes-
man said the situation along the
newly restored northern U. N.
defense line late yesterday was
much improved"


Correspondent Erickson reported
yesterday that the main force of
the most recent Red offensive
against the northern wall had
been spent. He warned that the
Reds were keeping up their pres
sure there. however.


1t. Gen. Walton H. Walker,
9th Army commander, said earlier
that the Red offensive which be-
gan September / was the largest
since the North Koreans invaded
the South June 25.


Gen Walker said last Sunday,
September 3. was his darkest day.
The Reds aimed savage blows at
both ends of the battle front on
that day. Both finally were stopped
cold.

MANILA. May 26.-Seventeen

killed today in the largest at
tempted prison break in the his
tory of the Philippines.


Five convictS and two guards
were wounded in the two-hour
gun battle that ensued after lunch.


The battle started when some
so long-term prisoners broke into
the prison armory while marching
from the dining hall. Some were
armed with knives and forks.
Others obtained machine guns
and rifles.


Guards opened fire on the build
ing. They set it and another
prison building on fire.


The armed convicts scattered
when the flames burst and battled
guards, constabularymen and reg
ular army troops for two hours.


No prisoners escaped, authori-
ties said.


Late today prison authorities
said they had rounded up some
of the ringleaders of the attempted
break.

SUWON. Korea, June % de-
layedl The North Korean Com
muniSt invaders of South Korea
have pressed a smart attack from
the beginning. They have used
good military tactics.


They showed crafty planning in
launching their offensive across
the 38th parallel Sunday.


Brig. Gen. William j. Roberts,
senior American military adviser
to the South Korean Army. had
just departed for the United States
and retirement.


For days the Reds had been
dickering with the south over an
exchange of political prisoners.
And they struck on a Sunday
when they knew a good many of
the field advisers of the American
military advisory group were in
Seoul.


They moved in what is generally
regarded as the rainy season.
Not a few Americans and Koreans
had thought the weather would
delay any plans the Reds might
have for a full-scale attack.


Once in action. the North
Koreans have used their Russian
built tanks well on the poor roads
which wind through this rugged,
mountainous country.


Red artillery outshoots in dis
tance the Southern guns which
therefore are in a poorer position
to resist the invaders.
Red mortar fire on Southern
positions has been good.
The Northerners probe ano
thrust for weak spots. And they
pour on the pressure when they
find one.


An admittedly quick survey OF
the military situation since my
arrival here today offers little
reason for optimism for the
South-unless they can get more
of everything.


They are looking to the United
States for that.

WASHINGTON - (ANP) - The

protection and extension OF civil
rights in the United States, accord
ing to the balance sheets just re-
leased by the American Jewish Con-
gress and the NAACP.


There was not only improved or
concerned with the fight for equal
ity, but the courts decided some IA
vorable victories, and public officials
manifested an increasing awareness
of their obligations to protect and
enlarge the civil rights of all groups
in the population, the report show
ed.


The states enacted more civil
rights laws last year then in any
previous year in the nations history.
Campaigns for anti-discrimination
legislation were conducted with
vary ing degrees of success in more
than 20 states.


-Four states enacted FEPC laws
during the year, bringing the num-
Der of states with effective legisla-
ton against employment in discrim.
ination to eight. New Jersey and
Massachusetts, banned discrimina-
ton in colleges, universities, trade
preparatory and other schools, while
New Jersey and Connecticut improv.
ed the legal procedure for prevent
ing discrimination in places of pub
lie accommodation. Six states pro.
hibited discrimination and segrega.
ton in the National Guard, while
three mid-Western states forbade
segregation in their public schools.
New York City and San Francisco
enacted ordinances forbidding dis.
elimination in publicly-assisted
housing. An anti-lynching law was
passed in Texas and an anti-KKK
mask law in Alabama. At least %
Southern cities also adopted anti
mask ordinances.


The civil rights issues were kept
before the public throughout the
year by means of the public press;
the motion picture industry, which
produced four important and serious
pictures dealing with various prob
lens facing Negroes in this coun.
try; and through the 20 books pub.
Hshed during the year which en-
phasized some aspect of group rela-
tons os their theme.

first plants to wake up in the
spring, sending up slender sharp

water.

cylindrical structures will have the
upper half finished off like that of
a cats tail. The staminate or male
flowers are massed at the top while
the pistillate flowers (female) form
the tail"


At this time the anthers are
packed to overf1owing with pollen,
this is sifted down with a passing
breeze and when a stronger wind
comes along the neighboring cat
tails are, given a generous busting.
Thus the pistillate flowers receive
ripe pollen from other flowers and
seed children are assured.


Each cat tail seed in autumn is
furnished with its own balloon on
which to travel to far away places.


Lower shorter leaves surround
the base of the plant, giving it
strength and size. All the leaves

ernments represented were Aus
tralia, India, Pakistan, Ceylon,

the Philippines.

ence seemed to fall far short of
binding the nations politically
into a closer regional unit.


When the conference first was
conceived by Philippines President
Elpidio Quirino, the announced
purpose was to form a union to
stem the rush of communism in
the Far East. Nationalist China
and South Korea hailed the idea.

and social lines mot against any,
body" Nationalist China and

ganization. The proposal emerged
heavily watered down. The dele
gates agreed to recommend to

Romulo communicate with them
regularly on progress of confer
ence recommendations.


Future negotiations, if any, will
be carried on through regular
diplomatic channels.

BERLIN, Sunday, Dec. 3.-Anti-
Communist Berliners swarmed to
the polls before dawn today. once
again to defy the Russians in this
encircled city.


AS the municipal election in the
Western sectors of the city got
under way at midnight, long lines
Of shabbily dressed voters already
were waiting as special stations
near the Soviet sector.


These were the ill-paid, often
threatened employees of Commu-
mist industries and enterprises,
who had been commanded to work
volunteer Sunday shifts" to keep
them from voting during the day.


Hurry it up," growled a switch
man from the Soviet-controlled
elevated railway as he and an
other switchman joined the voters
line. We've got to be back on the
job at 4 am"


Sign Brings Wry Jokes.


Others-charwomen. machin-
lists, clerks and stevedores-joked
wryly about the newest Com
munist sign to deck the Branden-
burg Gate on the Soviet-sector
border.


American splitter election tor
lures Berlin anew" the sign said.


Police in the West sectors jailed
81 Red agitators yesterday, rails
ing the weeks total to 269. But
no violence was reported this
morning when the election, bitter
ly denounced by the Russians and
the Communists, started AS in
the days Of the Berlin blockade,
the issue was whether to defy
Communism agin.


Youths Aid Propaganda.


The Soviet Control Commission
and the East German Communist
government continued a mammoth
propaganda campaign to frighten
Berliners away from the polls.


Speeding carloads of Commu-
mist Free German Youth" tossed
expensively printed four-color
leaflets about the streets late
last night. The leaflets called the
Western nations 'warmongers'
who want to attack Russia"


But election officials, surveying
early morning crowds at the
polling places, predicted more than
80 per cent of the eligible Ber-
liners would turn out to repudi-
ate Communism.


Before the polls close at pm,
1t is expected that most of the
1.664,722 enfranchised citizens in
the allied sectors will cast ballots


Reuter- Appeals for Vote.

choosing their representatives

parties. City and district assembly
seats totaling $40 are at stake.


A Soviet-sponsored Communist
demand that citizens boycott the
polls smothered all party issues,
however.


Socialist Mayor Ernst Reuter-
and all his political rivals united
last night in warning that who
ever fails to vote, votes Commu-
MIST" Mr.. Reuter- appeared cer-
tain that at least 80 per cent will
turn out.


ROit Squads Ready.


-Four thousand police riot squad
members stood guard to protect
voters from threatened Commu-
mist violence.


Police Chief Johannes Stumm
had the remainder of his 13,50O-
man force on the alert for trouble.
But Red tactics seemed confined to
hit-and-run raids by young agi-
tators. who argued on street cor
ners with passers-by.

exhaust pipe was clogged with
mud. The Clinton resident didn't

A Nation wide spot check by the

highly variegated impact on sales

One main fact stands out
people have cut back their heavy

That is exactly what the Re-

There has been lot of talk lately about
bridge bottlenecks but the biggest bridge tieup
of all is the one which has developed between
the District Commissioners and the National
Capital Park and Planning Commission over
new Anacostia bridge. Long suffering victims
of both varieties of tieups will welcome the pros
pect of a congressionally enforced end to the
battle of the bridges" A House District Sub
committee has laid the groundwork for cessation
of the battle in approving the East Capitol
Street Bridge bill sponsored by the Commits
sioners.


1t is not surprising that the subcommittee,
after hearing both sides of the controversy,
decided in favor of the East Capitol street plan.
The District Highway Department made out
good case for that location, as against the
NCPPC- C-proposed Massachusetts Avenue Bridge.
The highway engineers presented impressive
traffic-count figures, charts and maps in support
of the Districts contention that the East Capitol
site would better serve immediate and future
traffic needs across the Anacostia than any other
bridge location. The Districts plan was strongly
indorsed by the Federal Bureau of Public Roads
and by Maryland highway authorities.


Opposition to the East Capitol site was based
chiefly on the argument that bridge there
would destroy longview plans for park develop
ment of that area. The bridge undoubtedly
would compel revision of the original East
Capitol program, but the Commissioners gave
the committee assurances that the bridge and
its approaches could be fitted into the park plan
without destroying any of the essential features.
The Commissioners specifically agreed to legls-
lative provso protecting the arboretum from
encroachment They denied that the proposed
stadium would be ruined, although they are
said to favor a different location for such a
traffic generating structure.


Reluctance of the planners to give up or
modify long standing park development plans
is understandable, but not necessarily persuasive.
The original plans~for construction OF monu-
mental Federal buildings along both sides of
East Capitol street already are in conflict with
the building decentralization program now advo-
Gated by the same planners. Changing condi-
tions-popuation and traffic trends and even
atomic warfare-have necessitated modification
of many of the city's building and parkway
plans Necessity will force further changes in
the future. Certainly necessitous conditions call
for immediate construction of another bridge
over the Anacostia between the Sousa and Ben
ming Bridges-and East Capitol street seems the
logical place for It,


Since it has become evident that the bridge
dispute is not likely to be settled by mutual
agreement of the opposing parties, Congress
should step in and stop the battle. The Davis
subcommittee has suggested good way to end
the squabble. The time has arrived for action
instead of words. For unless a decision Is
reached while the District appropriation bill still
is pending, the chance for start this year on
the urgent task of building new bridge over
the Anacostia will go up in the smoke of dis
sension.
headline: To End the Battle of the Bridges

TRIPOLI.-What are they going to
Il do with Tripoli, the pearl of the
Duce's former empire?


Modern, immaculate. and practically
made by hand, this city is the biggest
asset in all the sandy waste from Tunisia
to the Western desert.


With the naval base at Benghazi and
the airdromes east of here, this place,
properly exploited, might finance the
United States of Libya, which the United
Nations General Assembly has decreed
must come into being by 1882.


Unless somebody produces good idea,
1t may go the way of the old Tripoli
and its sister towns of Leptis Magma
and Sabratha, whose ruins may now be
seen sticking out of the sands q few
miles from here.


There still is time. The British, who
have occupied the place since the 9Th
Army came through in 1943, have kept
it fairly tidy. The hotels are intact,
together with dozens of fine apartment
buildings with bathrooms that really
work-f1ne restaurants and handsome
public buildings.


Morally, the Italian colonial program
was terrible. 1t did nothing for the
natives, except for few noisy gestures,
and it robbed them blind.


But architecturally it was inspired by
the noble ideas of ancient Rome. and
Tripoli got the full benefit.


In the '30S the city was a pint-sized
combination of Rome. Monte Carlo and
Gomorrah. 1t had two gambling casinos,
% official houses of i'll fame-cabarets,
chic hotels. restaurants all over the
place. and lively and prosperous popu-
lation of Italians.


Pleasure cruises touched here, people
flew from the continent for week ends
and money poured into the place.


There are still about $4,000 Italians
living here. and some of the $4,000
Italians who still farm the hinterland

marked for assassination by Com
munist-led plotters.


French authorities said the Wet
Namese police had arrested num-

ordered to prepare the plot against
Mr.. Heath's life. They were mem
berS of Moscow-trained Ho Chi
Minis Wet Mini guerrillas, the
French said.


Previously, the 55-year -old
Heath, Minister to Bulgaria until
that country's Communist regime
ordered him out for alleged spy
ing, has had two bodyguards from
the French and Wet Namese
police. The Marines arrived here
last week.

target for propaganda blasts from
the Wet Mini radio in connection

government. A fourth shipload of

now from the American freighter
Steel Voyager.

SEATTLE, Sept. "A quickly
made blinker signal sped the
rescue early today of an excursion
boat and it's 800 passengers.


The 120-ton Virginia v was
stranded and blacked out in Puget
Sound after boiler tube blew out,
cutting off all power.


The vessel was towed into Lake
Union and berthed safely 21a
hours after it blinked its first call
for aid. 1t broke down 10 miles
north of Seattle.


Two Seattle men, who had
learned blinker signaling in the
Navy, quickly improvised blinker
light and attracted the fishing boat
Marpet. They are Jim Murphy
and Jack Giorgetti,, who were pas
sengers on the Virginia v.


Another passenger, Frank Bo-
Earth of Seattle. went aboard the
Marpet and radioed for aid.


Early reports had the veteran
Puget Sound ship drifting and
listing heavily. But Capt. James
Henshaw, skipper with the Foss
Launch & Tugboat Co., said only
a slight list was apparent when
his crew put line aboard.


All of the passengers, en- route
back from a days outing in the
San Juan Islands, were reported in
high spirits"

HANOVER, Germany, June
1.-THE Soviet zone of Germany
was 40 acres larger today and the
British zone 40 acres smaller in a
neat bit of Communist land re-
form.


German survey officials of the
Soviet zone simply picked up bor-
der markers, carried them west
ward, and set them down.


They said this corrected the
border to the old line that divided
the provinces of Hanover and
Prussia.


Then they divided up the land,
mostly owned by a British zone
resident, Count Won der Schulen-
burg, among residents of the So
Wet zone town of Breitenrode to
use for farming.


British officials refused to get
excited.


"The Soviet zone Germans
have made similar border changes
before" said a British spokesman,
usually, their German counter
parts in the British zone just move
the markers back where they came
from"


Count Schulenburg, equally un-
perturbed about the wandering
border, made the same comment.


The 40 acres consist solely of
farmland, without buildings.

FRANKFURT, Germany, Sept.
30.-A substantial majority of
West Germans have confidence in
American determination to stand
firm against further Communist
aggression and to defend Germany
in case of war. a public opinion
survey by the United States High
Commission showed today.


Even before the United Nations
launched its counteroffensive in
Korea, most Germans had faith
in ultimate Western victory there,
the survey showed.


Most West Germans prefer to
side with the West rather than
stay neutral or side with the Rus
slams. However, the number pre-
ferring neutrality increased from
one fourth to one third since the
Korean war began.


Despite Communist propaganda,
nearly all West Germans are con-
vinced that the North Korean at
tack was instigated by Russia.

the stock market today.

hand picked group of high-grade
stocks which have recently been
heavily favored. Losses running

Business picked up speed rapidly
on the way down and contracted
as the market Steadied.

Ways and Means Committee tc

increase was voted late yesterday

hem Steel. Republic Steel. Gen
eral Motors. Chrysler. American

A piano program built along
new lines, without the usual list
ing of standardized compositions,
was given by Anthony Chanaka,
the well-known resident pianist,
in the Phillips Gallery last night.


The artist put his best foot for
ward by opening the recital with
Aaron Copland's powerful so
nata," which presumably received
its first performance here.


Not unlike a broad canvas, the
work represents substantial piece
OF serious music, dramatic and
deeply felt. Its majestic dissonant
chords became meaningful under
the strong and agile fingers of
Mr.. Chanaka, who did not spare
himself to make his reading elo-
quent. AS the sonata progressed,
no doubt was left that the COM
poser had message which he re-
lated in a succession of episodes,
the intriguing 'Scherzo" being one
of these. It's half questioning
half mocking contents relieved
much of the emotional intensity
with which the first and last
movements are permeated. The
audience was in a receptive mood
and signif1ed its approval by pro-
longed applause.


Three classical numbers: Bulls
"The Kings Hunting Jigg," Birds
"Pavana" and Handel's "Gavotte
with Variations" charmingly
played, separated the American
work from the French, which
formed the balance of the pro-
gram. OF these, the least inter-
esting was Faure's Theme and
Variations, op. 49," somewhat too
stolidly presented to make the
most OF its graceful style. But
Mr.. Chanaka's bold execution of
Poulenc's movement Perpetuel''
recaptured for him his hold on
the assembly which extended fur
ther to the three selections that
followed: Presto" promenade
and "Toccata," by the same COM
poser.

CUZCO, Peru. May 23.-Offers
of help came from all parts of
the Americas today for this thou
sand-year -old city, digging itself
out of earthquake -Strewn rubble
which was expected eventually to
yield so or more bodies.


From Ss far away as Washing
ton and Santiago. Chile. came
sympathy and aid for the sur
vivors of the violent quake SUM-
day which left centuries-old his
toric buildings in ruins.


President Flying to City.


Peru's President. Brig. Gen.
Manuel Odria. with his ministers
of public education and public
works, was flying here today from
Lima after a cabinet meeting yes
terday which voted million soles
tabout 5000 ,000D for relief and re-
habilitation.


Six transport planes loaded with
relief supplies and workers al
ready had been sent from Lima.


AS workers continued to search
the rubble of the city. 43 bodies
had been recovered. City officials
said the death list was expected
to total at least SO. About $50
were injured.


The brief shock left ancient
churches and Scme of CuZco's
most beautiful historic buildings
in ruins.


Inca Ruins Undisturbed.


The huge Inca ruins in the
stricken city were not disturbed
by the quake. But the Church of
Santo Domingo, an architectural
gem built alongside the ancient
Inca Temple of the Sun. was left
a heap of ruins. Other historic
religious buildings also were badly
damaged.


Peru's Minister of Public Health,
Col. Alberto Lopez, arrived yes
terday to direct relief work. The
Colombian and Bolivian Red
Cross, the Pan-American Sanitary
Office in Washington and other
agencies in the hemisphere sent
offers of assistance.


President Truman and Chile's
President, Gabriel Gonzalez vi
della, cabled messages of con-
dolence and offered help.

TOKYO, Aug. 5.-B-29s bombed
the Seoul railroad yards today for
the second straight day. leaving
them flaming and shrouded in
smoke.


The B-29s, flying from Japan,
dropped 100 tons of bombs on
the yard. Yesterday it was 80
tons.


In the central sector of the
South Korean front. American
planes blasted a large enemy ar
mored force one-half mile west
of the Naktong River defense line.
Associated Press Correspondent
Left Erickson said the American
planes knocked out four of five
tanks moving northeast toward
Waegwan and pounded Red ar
tillery, trucks and troops.


American artillery also hurled
shells into the convoy.


Yesterday set a new record for
the busy Air Force-a total of $50
flights within "a hours, mostly
against enemy soldiers and their
supply lines.


Four villages were burned out
and planes plastered napalm fire
bombs on the previously undam-
aged sections of Chinju, jumping
off place for the Reds push from
the west against Pusan, main
United States supply port.


Napalm bombs, made of jellied
gasoline, spread intensely hot
flame over the area where they
hit.


Chinju is SIS miles west of the
port city. Pilots reported the Reds
were building up a force there.


Land and carrier based United
States Marine fighters joined with
light bombers, F-80 jets and Mus
tangs in sweeping up and down
the front, hitting at troops and
supplies as the Reds moved
toward the main Allied defense
line.


A 5th Air Force spokesman said
the planes flew 452 combat sor-
ties, a record for a single day.
Strategic and reconnaissance sor-
ties raised the total number of
individual flights for the day to
$50.


Fifteen night intruder missions
were flown by fighters and bomb
ers in an effort to impede the
night movement of Red supplies
and troops. The night flyers
ranged from Sunchon, on the
southwest coast, northward to
the Red-held capital of Seoul.

former Wet Mini stronghold 40

the Wet Mini in the sparse noun
tain region, the French hope to
dissipate Wet Mimi strength.
Aside from the strategic i'm
portance. Thai Nguyen commands

thus denies the Wet Mimi in

Allied officials are deeply con-
cerned because the West German
government is neglecting threat

preoccupation with international
affairs.

Big Ben's throaty roar atop

Charley Titone's ability to take
punishment saved him last night
in the main bout at Turner's
Arena. The Brooklyn feather
weight was battered around rather
freely by the unorthodox Luis
Ramos of Puerto Rico in the early
going, but after weathering this
furry Titone came back to win
handily.


Ramos, shooting fast hooks from
both sides and displaying a gen.
eral brawling style of fighting

rounds, particularly in the third
when the Brooklyn boy was rocked
back. Titone back-pedaled to
keep out of serious trouble and
coming out for the fourth started
keeping Ramos away with left
jabs.


After that Titone's classier box
ing took control of the match and
he won the unanimous decision.

weight from New York. added to
his knockout string by stopping
Washington's Ben Harrison in the
fourth round. At that, Harrison
proved tougher than Wallace's
previous opponents and absorbed
some solid jaunts before folding.
Seven previous Wallace opponents
had gone away in the first or sec
ond round.


Another knockout in the prelims
was scored by Jimmy Balderson
in 81 seconds of the first round
over Johnny Fields. In other pre-
Inns. Tommy Bohak deciSioned
Jimmy Sewell. Jimmy Briscoe won
over Frank Ball and Holly Minis
outpunched Johnny Pratt.

remote mountain region, about
300 miles northeast of Lima, said
Mr.. Harrah suffered a frozen foot
and Mr.. Maxwell a frozen toe
when they were forced to spend
the night on the mountain with
out shelter.


The men are due here today
for treatment.

A rather common error among
newspaper writer's is the use of
the wrong auxiliary verb in SEN
tenceS containing two or more
clauses. Here is an example from
the current news: Fifty five
buildings were damaged and one
plane destroyed"


Now obviously the plural "Were"
cannot be carried forward to serve
the clause "and one plane (were?)
destroyed" The clause must have
it's own singular verb, thus: Fifty
five buildings were damaged and
one plane was destroyed


Wrong: "One was killed and
three injured"


Right: One was killed and three
were injured.


Wrong: -Four oil wells have
turned into great craters and pro-
duction killed" One is prompted
to ask: Production killed what?
The second clause is meaningless
without It's own auxiliary verb.

said.


Wholesale pork prices also have
increased between 2 and 4 cents
a pound.


Wholesale meat dealers said
beef prices usually advance in the
spring, but this weeks price in
crease was abnormally high.

did not know what was causing
the shortage in the Chicago mar
ket although they had heard that
Government purchasing agents
were buying heavily.


Chain store officials said beef
and pork on sale this week end
was purchased before the whole
sale price advanced. Next week,
they said, they will have to jump
their prices.

Washington today.


Mail deliveries. which years ago
ran as high as four Q day IN the
downtown area. had dwindled to
one-an economy measure ordered
By Postmaster General Donaldson
and designed TO save $400. 900 an
nually In Washington alone.


Actually. there will be two de-
hveries for the strictly business
area. but the average citizens will
get mail only once-usually In the
morning.


The economy move eventually
may mean dropping 81 temporary
clerks and transferring 125 car
riers to clerical duties. Personnel
changes will be more gradual than
was indicated earlier. Assistant
Postmaster w. Gordon Bell said.


Closed business windows in the
main postofnce yesterday marked
the first visual sign Of the money
saving program. The stamp. gen.
eral delivery. parcel post, infor-
nation and other windows will be
closed on Sundays and holidays.


PoStmen began their routes ut
$3.50 am. today-an nour earlier
than under the two-a-day deliv-
cry plan. although some residents
may still not receive their mail
until afternoon.

centers.

French warplanes struck hard
today at Langson, big Indo- Chi

French troops last Wednesday.


A French military spokesman
said the planes hit gasoline and
oil tanks. Ammunition and food
stocks left behind by the French
also were bombed, he said, to
keep them from the Wet Mini

Mini.


French sources said air attacks
on the former French headquar-
ters base began Friday.

The French garrison was Or

before it could complete its demo-
lition work. ..


The French spokesman reported
Wet Mini attacks still were
underway in the vicinity of Tien-
yen, key French post and supply
center in the middle of new 100
mile long frontier defense line.


Several French posts guarding
Tienyen have been harrassed by
Wet Mini units.


The French spokesman seid Wet
Mini troops captured one small
post Friday from Indo- Chinese
auxiliary troops The post was To-
Gated between Tienyen and Mon
cay. on the coast. 1t was retaken
later in a French counter-attack,

The spokesman said the French
high command believes the most
immediate threat now is to the
isolated frontier post of Laokay,
$50 miles northwest of Hanoi.
Wet Mimi concentrations already
are massed in the region.


The bastion guards one of the
four main invasion routes into
North Indo-China and is astride
the partially demolished Kun
ming-Haiphong railroad.


Meanwhile, French troops were
attempting to consolidate the
northwestern flank of their new
rectangular defense perimeter in
North Indo-China.


A series of operations was
launched to clear Wet Mimi units
from the important communica-

on the frontier through Phulang-

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, April
25.-A heavily armed Russian
minesweeper chased a Swedish
trawler all the way from a point
"a miles of the Polish coast to
the edge of Swedish territorial
waters in the Baltic Sea, the news
paper Morgentidningen reported
today.


The Swedish craft was the
Larex, out of Soelvesborg, the
same ship which was seized by
Soviet patrol boats in the Baltic
last February.


A Swedish Foreign Office spokes-
man said he had mo official
knowledge" of the incident.
Sweden has made repeated repre-
sentations to the Soviet Union
about the extension of Soviet ter
ritorial waters in the Baltic and
Soviet harassment of Swedish
vessels. The Russians claim a
12-mile limit, while no other
Baltic state claims more than a
3-to-6-mile limit.


The newspaper said the trawler
had been salmon fishing in the
open sea when the Russian mine
sweeper bore down. The Swedish
skipper, Alrik Johannson, left his
nets behind and lit out for Sweden.


With the minesweeper in its
wake-sometimes no more than Is
yards away-the Larex raced some
rs miles across the open sea until
it reached Swedish territorial wa
ters outside Gotland. when the
minesweeper ended it's pursuit, the
paper said.


The Larex entered the port of
Karlskrona yesterday and the
crew was questioned by police and
ordered not to discuss the incident
with the press, the paper said. It
added that the Karlskrona police
were preparing a report for the
Foreign Office.


The Larex and another Swedish
! vessel, the Marion, were seized by
> Soviet patrol boats February 20
about 80 miles off the Soviet-helc
coast of East Prussia. The boats
were detained two weeks.
Fishermen's organizations have
been urging naval escorts fol
Swedish fishing vessels in the Bal
tic because of such incidents.

MADRAS, India-The failure
of the monsoon for the third sue
cessive year has left this south
Indian state with a critical situa-
ton. Lakes are dry, crops have
withered and cattle are starving.
Some farmers are migrating. The
price of rice has tripled in the
black market and rice rations are
down to less than seven ounces
a day. Official estimates are that
8 million people have been af-
fected by the scarcity of food.


Food officials have tried to sup
plement the rice ration with
wheat, milo and millet. But rice
eaters don't like these grains, and
it has not been possible to provide
adequate stocks, anyway.

CAIRO. Egypt. june 22.-The
seven Arab League Nations told
the United States. Britain and
France today that the Western
Big Three plan to arm the Middle
East against aggression is gener-
ally satisfactory TO them.


Western diplomats were openly
jubilant over the friendly tone Of
the joint reply from Egypt, Syria,
Lebanon. Iraq. Saudi Arabia, Jor-
dan and Yemen. They had feared
the governments might veer
toward the line of the isolationist
press which has charged the Big
Three with interfering with ma
tional sovereignty.


Jordan is bound by the league
reply although King Abdullah
boycotted the League sessions be-
cause of the refusal of other Arab
states to recognize his annexation
OF Eastern Palestine.


Copies Of the reply were sent to
the Ambassadors of the Big Three.
Their governments had an
nounced on May IS a guarantee of
the Middle East's national
frontiers against forceful changes
and said they would provide ARAB
nations and Israel with arms to be
used only for defense and internal
security.


Much Of the nine-point reply
became known before the League
adjourned Saturday.


The Arab countries crisply noted
that they "are not prepared to ad-
NIT any action which might cause
prejudice to their sovereignty or
independence" But generally the
reply was aimed to put into writ
ing the Interpretation of the Big
Three plan that had been given
by Western diplomats.

Francis (Reds) Bagnell, Penn
football captain and backfield ace
has been named the country's
outstanding college football player
of 1850 by the Maxwell Memorial
Football Club.


The announcement was made
yesterday by Bert Bell, National
Football League commissioner
and president of the Maxwell club
Bell said Bagnell would receive
the organizations annual award
January 9.


Bagnell led the eastern inter-
collegiate ground gaining parade
with a total of 1910 yards, only
seven off the all-time record set
by Columbia's Paul Governali in
1942. He scored nine touchdowns
and threw six touchdown passes
during the season.


Bagnell, 14th player to be hon
ored by the Maxwell club, also
set national single season rec
ord when he tossed SO passes be-
fore one was intercepted. This
streak was broken on his third
pass attempt against unbeaten
and united Army.

ace and current end for the De-
troit Lions in the NFL, won the

LAYTON, Okla, Jan. 27.-Five
small children burned to death
alone in their flimsy two-room
frame house here yesterday. The
structures only door accidentally
became locked and thwarted
frantic resuce efforts by their 23-
year-old mother.


Seven persons escaped unhurt
from another two-room hut
damned. against the burning
building.


The victims, ranging from 2
months to years, were the chill
dren of MIR. and Mrs. C. D. Young.


Mrs. Young said she stepped out
: into the yard to get water from
a hydrant and stopped few
minutes to talk with neighbor
Then the screams from her chill
dren brought her racing to the
door, only to find the inside wood
en- latch had dropped into place


She tried to reach the children
by breaking WINDOWS, but each
time the heat drove her and help
ing neighbors back.


Mr.. Young, a 32-year old truck
driver, was at work when the
tragedy occurred.

ran from the adjoining. house
when flames began seeping
through the wall. A piece of blaz-

burned him slightly as he, finally
forced the door open.

ting the fire.

BERLIN, Oct. 21.-The United
States High Commission news
paper, Neue Zeitung, said today
five persons were killed in a clash
between uranium miners and So
Wet zone police at Johanngeor-
genstadt, SaXony.


The report, unconfrmed by
other information sources, said the
incident occurred several days ago
when the miners, returning home
from work in a Russian operated
uranium concession, overloaded a
train.


The miners refused to obey a
station masters request to get of
the roof OF the railway cars and
police opened fire, the paper said.
After several miners had been
wounded the miners seized the
station master and four policemen
and beat them to death, Neue
Zeitung said.

NEW YORK, April 15.-The

helplessly tonight in the Atlantic
Ocean toward Sable Island off the
coast of Nova Scotia.

dispatched the tug guard. The
stricken vessel is wallowing about
140 miles east of the Canadian
port. -Four American Coast Guard
cutters were also alterted to stand
by in case the Federal Trader needs
more help than the tug can pro-
vide.


The Nova Scotia coastline
stretches from the southwest to
the northeast, with Sable-a long
narrow reef-south of it's upper
tip. The helpless ship is between
the mainland and the island, and
is being driven directly offshore
toward Sable. The island has a
history as maritime graveyard.

HONOLULU, Oct. 28.-Three
American cruisers were heading
home today from the Korean war


Admiral Arthur w. Radford
Pacific Fleet commander, an
nounced the 13,600- ton heavy
cruisers Toledo and Helena and
the light cruiser Worcester are
due in Pearl Harbor Thursday.


They were the first major
American fleet units to leave the
Korean theater since the war be-
gan.


The ships will take on fuel and
supplies in Pearl Harbor. The
Toledo and Helena will proceed
to West Coast ports while the
Worcester heads for the East
Coast, via the Panama Canal.


The Helena and Toledo passed
through Pearl Harbor July II en-
route to the Orient. The Wor-
cester left the Mediterranean via
the Suez Canal for the Far East
July 81.

HONG KONG, Aug. 1.-THE
British destroyer Concord and
Chinese shore batteries fought a
Commute gun duel today in the
second clash between British war
ships and Red artillerymen on the
approaches to Hong Kong.


After the Concord battle it was
officially reported the navy frigate
Whitesand Bay exchanged fire Au-
gust 2 with gun emplacements on
Lingting Island.


The Concord fought with bat
teries on three islands-Taitami,
Puntin and Lingting. Her cap
tain said she fired in self defense
after Red batteries opened up.


Royal Navy officers said there
was one minor casualty and no
damage to the ship as it steamed
into Hong Kong.


Red shore batteries have been
quick to fire on ships recently. On
three successive days last week
merchant ships were shelled. They
were British, American and Nor
wegian.


It was estimated the Reds fired
three FOUNDERS at H.M.S. Concord.
The destroyer fired much more
powerful AZ inch guns.


This was the first reported ex-
change Of gunfire between a Brit
ish warship and the Chinese Com
since April, 1949. At that
time, the cruiser London, the de-
stroyer Consort and the frigates
Black Swan and Amethyst came
under Communist shore fire in the
Yangtze. River. In all, 43 British
sailors were killed and more than
80 wounded in the 1949 engage
ment.

Riviera night, Trant put his hand against

To his right, down the short strip of dock,
he could see the lighted Casino. In the

wharf

Then, suddenly, from the sailboat behind
him, he heard faint scuff1ing sound. He
spun around just in time to see crouched

lightly from the bow of the white sailboat
onto the front deck of the cruiser.


With anxiety, he realized that the hus-
band had outsmarted them. He had ignored
the obvious route along the wharf and had
stolen back to the cruiser by jumping from
one moored boat to the next. Trant sprang
up the gangplank crossed the cruisers deck
and scrambled down the companionway.

banged. calling: Look out. He's coming
from the 'front.'"

ans scream followed by shot, There was
confused humping inside the cabin and then
a second shot. He hurled himself against
the door. 1t did not yield A faint moaning
sounded inside. Then key turned and
slowly the door opened inward.


The girl was standing there, the dark hair
tumbling around a face blanched with horror.

ampton dock today in a bowling
gale that lashed Western Europe

Most of the liners 622 passen-

cluded automobiles.


Crewmen stuffed mattresses into

men helped to push them into

Water was allowed into the star

Workmen then fitted temporary
wooden patches over the holes
preparatory to moving the Wash
ington into drydock tomorrow.


Sixty mile an hour winds
stranded the Cunard liner Queen
Mary in Cherbourg Harbor with
1,848 passengers aboard. The big
ship was unable to approach the
docks in a raging sea.


The gale snarled shipping,
tossed the sea over sea walls and
flooded coastal roads in many
parts of Great Britain. Rivers
overfiowed at several coastal
points. Miles of fields were sub
merged.

leak in the hull by making tenn

roof. They were preparing to jump
of. Mr.. Glass and his patrol car
companion-who meanwhile had

was blasted with such force that

aprons but at least one resident
heard it. He didn't note the hour.


The safecrackers entered the
building. through a delivery chute,
police said. The paddock on the
chute door was pulled apart, then
apparently put together again.


The loot was in bills and silver.

George Washington University
today signed a contract to play
all Its home basket ball games at
Uline Arena for the next three
years.


Georgetown University is ex-
pected to sign a similar contract
after several minor details are
ironed out. The Two schools thus
move their basket ball games from
the Armory scene of most of their
games the past two seasons.


The contract for George Wash
ington was signed by Max Far
rington, director of mems activi-
ties for the school, and by Maj
Howard Livingston, representing
the Uline Arena management.


No Conflict With Pros.


The college games will be played
on Tuesday and Friday nights
and thus will avoid conflict with
the professional games played on
Wednesday and Saturday nights
For the last two years. both the
pros and colleges have been COM
peting with each other for busi-
ness on Wednesday and Saturday
nights.


Main reason for the shift. ac-
cording to harrington, was the
lack of adequate seating facilities
at the Armory. He pointed out
that the colleges had to hire their
own seats and that they were of
an unsatisfactory circus bleacher
type. He also pointed out that
the Armory was not available for
all the dates the schools wanted


There have been rumors that
we were being kicked out of the
Armory, or that we got sore and
left, but neither is true" said Far
rington. 'The management OF
the Armory, Dutch Bergman
Frank Hayes and the rest have
been very friendly and co-opera-
tive, but they could not overcome
the seating situation"


Dates Well Arranged.


In returning to Uline Arena
the colleges 60 back to the place
where they played before shifting
to the Armory. They left Uline
Arena because of what they called
excessive rentals and inability
to get satisfactory dates. They
now have what harrington said
was "a very satisfactory contract
and an excellent arrangement on
dates. With the colleges playing
on Tuesdays and Fridays, and the
pros on Wednesdays and Satur-
days, it will make Uline Arena
the real center of basketball in
Washington"


Among the teams George Wash
ington will play at Uline Arena
next year are North Carolina
State, North Carolina, Washing
ton and Lee, Virginia. Duke, Will
liam and Mary, Virginia Tech
South Carolina, Clemson, Mary
land and Georgetown. Altogether
the schools expect to play from
IL to Is home games each at
Uline Arena, with five or six OF
them in double headers.

A raging three-alarm fire early
today destroyed the giant Fort
Myer field commissary building,
containing the posts new $4,000
meat refrigeration unit.


Arlington County and Fort
Myer firemen waged a five-hour
battle to bring the flames under
control. At 7 am. smoke still
was rising from the ruins.


The blaze broke out at about 2
am. in the center of the 2O0-foot-
long brick structure, which is near
the Fort Myer fence on Lee boule-
ward. Dozens of motorists pulled
over to watch flames pouring
from the roof. which sent columns
Of smoke and burning particles
hundreds of feet into the air.


Gas Feeds Blaze.


Fort Myer officials said about
two-thirds of the building was
taken up by the meat packing
and refrigeration unit, which held
the posts entire meat supply. A
small amount of canned goods
was stored in the other portion
Of the building.


Firemen said highly -infiam-
mable refrigeration gas kept feed
ing the blaze, and new columns
of smoke poured out as the entire
building was enveloped in flames.
Firemen extinguished fires started
on the roofs of two adjoining
buildings.


The early-morning fire brought
hundreds of servicemen from bar
racks in the area. Some assisted
in the flre-fighting and others
removed vehicles from garages
nearby.


Cause Not Determined.


Post officials said the meat re-
frigeration unit had been installed
only last spring.


Only injury reported. fire off,
cials said. was an injured hand
suffered by Arlington Fireman
Harry Leep when he slipped on ice.


Cause of the blaze. Fort Myer
officials said today, has not been
determined.

emerge the successor to President
Luis Battle Berres.


Mayo Gutierrez now is vice.
president. Martinez Trueba, ex-
mayor of Montevideo, was backed
by President Battle Berres.

NEW YORK, Oct. THE 1850
Yankees. lacking the luster Of
more prominent predecessors but
fearful foes nevertheless for the
powerless Phillies, quietly annexed
their 18th world baseball cham
pionship today by defeating the
Whiz Kids. to 2.


The Yanks thus won the world
series in four straight games. They
won the clincher before 68,098 un-
excited fans at Yankee Stadium.


While the Whiz Kids fizzled, the
Yankees moved to victory behind
the polished pitching of 21-year-
old Ed Ford, rookie left handler.
The youngster pitched magnifi-
Gently, but was deprived of shut
out when an outfield error paved
the way for the Phillier to score
their two runs after two men were
out in the ninth. Ford was taken
from the game. but got credit for
the win.


Story Book Climax.


Winning the final game was the
climax of story-book experience
for Ford. Joining the team in
June, he won nine games and lost
only one during the regular sea-
son and climaxed his brilliant
record with today'S victory.


For the sixth time in their IT
World Series appearances, the
Yankees swept the affair in four
games. In recent years, the Yanks
have dominated the annual fall
clash between the American and
National League pennant win
ners, taking nine in the last Is
years.


The Phillies. like their 1915
predecessors were not inspiring.


In 1915, they won the first
game against Boston, then lost
four straight, each by a margin
OF one run. Before today's rather
drab game, the Phillies also had
lost three successive games by one
run.


Today the Phils were out of
contention almost before the
customers settled in their seats.
The Yankees scored two runs in
the first inning off jittery Bob
Miller. They added three in the
sixth when Yogi Berra slammed
a home run off Jim Konstanty to
spark the uprising.


Pitching Won Series.


New York owed its sweep of the
series to its pitching. The Yam
KEGS got two-hitter from Vic
Raschi in the first game to win.
10. They received a seven-hit
game from Allie Reynolds to win
the second game, 81, in 10 in
nlngs. In the third game, Ed
Lopat and Tom Ferrick held the
PhllS to two runs while the Yanks
made three and today Ford should
have had a shutout.


Not since 1905, when Christy
Mathewson and Iron Man Joe
McGinnity held the Athletics to
three runs in five games, did a
World Series team display less
potency than the Phils. They
scored only five runs in four games

The Nations beef producers are

mand for meat will remain good
for several years to come.


The cattlemen's confidence in
the future is being expressed by
wide withholding of cattle from
the current slaughter market with
its favorable prices. Some cattle
being kept on ranges and farms
will be used for breeding purposes
to increase beef cattle numbers
for slaughter two and three years
from now. Also some are being
held for further fattening.


Helping to give the cattlemen
confidence is the prospect of pro-
longed heavy Government buying
under the national defense pro-
gram.


The Agriculture Department
said today meat production for
the winter season may reach its
peak about the middle of this
month.


That would mean a reduction
In consumer supplies in the first
quarter of 1851. Compared with
the same quarter last year there
may be little more pork, about
the same quantity of beef, less
veal, lamb and mutton.


Farm prices as a whole have in
creased about IL per cent since
the war started in Korea. But
most commodities are still below
price control levels authorized by
law.

showed that farm products ad-
vanced 8 per cent between mid
October and November to put
them within about 10 per cent of
the record level set in January,
1948.

averaged S per cent above parity.

following producers were bring

peanuts, hogs. potatoes, butterfat,
milk. barley, dry beans, oats, rye,
grain sorghums. soybeans, sweet
potatoes, grapefruit, oranges.

turkeys.

for more than their respective
parity prices were f1ue cured

beef cattle. lambs and veal calves.

calves. sheep, lambs and wool

other buildings.


The central buildings we're splin-

ANCHORAGE, Alaska, Aug. 5.
Recent unexplained explosions
on or near Russian-owned Big
Diomede Island in the Bering
Strait were reported today.


Mr.. and Mrs. Frank Morgan, of
Anchorage, returned yesterday
with the report from Little Dio-
mede Island. owned by the United
States and only miles from the
Soviet Far East island outpost.


The Morgans said that several
times during a four-month stay on
Little Diomede they heard loud
noises at sea. They believed the
noises may have been from a sur
vey ship taking soundings or from
the Siberian mainland. Fog pre-
vented them from locating the
sources.


The Morgans doubted that the
Russians are bolstering Big Dio-
mede as Eskimos reported that
only one Soviet plane was on the
island last winter.


The natives also reported that
the Russian island was strangely
inactive. Mr.. Morgan said. Last
spring, tourists said the island was
being evacuated of it's residents as
the Russians prepared to construct
a large base on Big Diomede. No
large construction is evident there,
Mr.. Morgan said.

3-year-old Judith Ann Payne was

charges against her parents and
two women of contributing to the
delinquency of a minor.


The little girl, reported missing
from her Ocean View home since
Sunday, was found in a tavern

he had read of the child's disap-

Domestic Relations court are her
parents, Elvin and Margaret
Payne: Mrs. Robert Provine, also
of Ocean View, and Shirley Mae
Olsen. unemployed waitress.


Police gave the following ver-
sion of the little girls troubles:


She was left with Miss Olsen.
a baby sitter, when her mother
reported to her waitress job Sun
day morning. Miss Olsen left
with the child that afternoon and
met Mrs. Provine Sunday night
at the tavern.


The two were sharing car.
Miss Olsen left the baby on the
back seat sometime during the
evening and did not return. Mrs.
Provine then took the little girl
home with her and kept her until
she was found at the tavern by
police.

enai River continued its ominous

without power off Cape May, N. j..

tian was sent from Cape May to
tow the Ludlow to New York.


Third Naval District headquar-
ters said that the ships lack of
power was due to mechanical fail
ure, but gave no details.


The 1,630-ton ship, called the
Lucky Lud" because she never
lost a man in the five invasions
she took part in during the war,
carried 236 naval reservists from
the Maine New Jersey area.


The ship experienced difficulty
on its trip south to San Juan,
Puerto Rico. arriving in port Ia
hours late and her water supply
nearly exhausted.


On the return trip her supply
of water again ran low and she
put into Charleston, S. c., for ad-
ditional stocks.

The Virginia State Board of Medical
the proposal to extend borderline reci-
procity to Washington physicians who are
summoned to treat patients in nearby
Virginia. The board has informed State
Senator Fenwick of Arlington that it not
only approves of such reciprocity in the
District area, but it believes similar privi-
leges should prevail along all other State
boundaries.


Senator FenWick and his fellow legiS-
lators from nearby Virginia are sponsoring
special legislation to end the disputes
which have arisen in the past over Vir-
ginias discriminatory licensing law. That
law, enacted many years ago, prevents
the State from giving District doctors the
same easy access to Virginia patients that
Virginia doctors enjoy under the Districts
liberal code. Because of the States insist
ence that District doctors desiring to
answer calls from patients in Virginia
must obtain the same fifty-dollar license
to practice that they would have to secure
If they were opening offices in the State,
District authorities have threatened to
cease granting Virginia doctors one-dol-
lar courtesy" privileges. Unless the Gen.
eral Assembly passes the reciprocity bill
the District will require all Virginia doc
tors to take out fifty-dollar Office licenses.


The Virginia law was designed to pro-
tect the State from activities of diploma
mill quackS. At the time of passage, many
States did not exercise the rigid control
over medical practice that now prevails.
But that day is past, and with it has gone
any real need for stringent State require
ments for examination and licensing of
physicians who have been granted licenses
in other States. 1t is to the interest of
Virginians living near the States bound
aries to make it easy for them to receive
medical service from out-of-State physi-
clans, not only in emergencies but when
ever the patients feel that they can benefit
from such treatment.

BELGRADE. Nov. Yugo.
slavia broke all but token diplo.
matte relations with tiny neigh.
boring Albania today as the result
of feud touched of by the
Russian-led Cominform's quarre.
with Premier-Marshal Tito.


A Yugoslav Information Minis
try spokesman said the Albanian
legation here has been CLOSED
and sealed" and simultaneously
made public the text Of a note
handed the Albanian representa-
tive here announcing both the
action and the reason for it.
The note charged Albania has
used the Belgrade legation not for
the conduct of current affairs
and for the settlement of existing
issues between the two govern
ments, but has utilized its exist
sence exclusively for the purposes
of conducting offending and pro-
vocative activities against Yugo-
slavia and its authority.


Not Wanted.


2 "Yugoslavia therefore consid-
ers the further sojourn of the rep
resentatiyes of Albania in Yugo-
slavia clearly useless" it said.


The move marked the most
spirited step Tito's government
has yet taken against any of the
Soviet satellites in retaliation for
a Moscow directed campaign
which has included an economic
boycott, political pressure and
diplomatic insults.


Yet it fell one step short of an
outright diplomatic break = at
least up to this point. The note
said Yugoslavia has chosen, the
legations of Yugoslavia and Al
bania in Budapest. Hungary, "for
the maintenance of. diplomatic
relations between the two coun-
tries"


To Receive Mail.


It said also that Yugoslavia was
prepared to receive diplomatic
mail from the Albanian govern
ment through any Albanian diplo-
matte mission or directly by
regular mail" Whether Albania
will accept these conditions re-
mains uncertain.


In effect, this means each
country will be without represen-
tatives in the others capital to
report first hand information on
the others affairs.


Except for the delivery Of the
diplomatic note, the latest de-
velopment in the Balkan cold war
OF nerves between this Com
inunist nation and her Communist
neighbors does not change the
situation much.


The Yugoslav legation in
Tirana. the Albanian capital, has
been closed since July as a result
OF what this country termed
persecution and discrimination
against Yugoslav diplomatic rep
resentatives. Albania has main
tanned only a skeleton staff here
for nearly two years.

VIENNA, Sept. 30. - Scattered


Communist disturbances brole


out for the third day in vienna


this morning as Russian-orsan-

-harass the Austrian government.


Communists seized control of

central part of the town.


One railroad station on the line
from Vienns to Bratislava, in
C1echoSlovakia. also was occupied
by Communist demonstrators
but the Austrian government
diverted trains by another route.
Spans Are Blocked.
The Danube bridges-one Of
which bears the name of the
Bridge of the Red Army''-were
. blocked by automobiles and Com
munists sitting astride the road.
In another Russian sector Reds
held up streetcar traffic for several
hours.


The demonstrations were all re-
stricted to Russian districts of
Vienna.


Austrian Chancellor DR.. Leo
pold Figls press officer said the
situation was much calmer than
in the last two days, during which
the Communists staged strikes,
demonstrations and traffic inter-
ruptions. They said they were
protesting government wage and
price increase.


Some Justification Seen.


Allied quarters said today the
Communists have some juStifica-
ton for their protests, since the
wage increases are not equal to
those of prices, particularly food.


There was a back-to-work
movement in many factories, al
though in some Russian-con-
troled factories workers remained
on strike.


Austrian sources said the Rus
slams apparently had given orders
that factories which had fulfilled
their production quotas could re-
main idle. Those, however, which
had failed to do so apparently
were ordered back to work. SINH
lar sporadic strikes were reported
throughout the country.


The Communist press threat
ened that factory shop stewards
from throughout Austria, at a
Communist called meeting in
Vienna Saturday. would urge the
workers on to more trouble.

Plan Hailed by Germans.

great step toward European
unity.

what sacrifices might be demanded

and steel output with that o1

European countries.


French Foreign Minister schu.

gested that talks on the project
be started in June by France, Brit.
ain, West Germany, Italy, Bel
gium, Holland and Luxembourg

French asked that the countries
go on record as favoring the pro-

TRENTON, N. J.-Regattas and
other water sports will highlight
the summer scene in New Jersey.


Sailboat regattas and speedboat
racing are on the maritime bill
of fare for vacation visitors
These will supplement New Jer-
sey's other water sports.


Twilight sailboat racing at
Wildwood by the-Sea for the reg
ular championship series OF
Thursday evening events, con-
tinues through September.


Model yachtsmen will have their
moment in the spotlight at Wee
quahic Park Lake in Newark when
the Irvington Model Yacht Club
runs its series of regattas, July /
to 3. The little vessels. some of
them marvelously ingenious re-
productions Of fine racing ships,
are a favorite with camera enthu-
siasts. Many attend the regatta
for the sole purpose of getting a
good collection of model boat
snapshots.


Stone Harbor will launch its
championship series of sailboat
races on July l and will continue
with similar events every week
during the season.


Inland resorts get into the
marine picture with the fourth
annual sailboat regatta sponsored
by the Businessmen's Association
of Netcong and the Netcong Stan
hope Rotary Club. The races be-
gin July 2 and will continue with
weekly meets until September 4
on the waters of Lake Musco-
netcong.


Cape May County's annual fish,
ing derby is already underway,
with thousands of fishermen vying
for the weekly awards given for
the best fish in all species.


Regular maritime diversions for
vacation visitors in New Jersey
include canoeing and rowing at
Belleplain State Forest and Hopat-
cong, Musconetcong and Parvin
State Parks.


New Jerseys most popular water
sport is still bathing. The coast
line is 120 miles long and hun
dreds of additional miles of water
frontage are added by more than
300 lakes, scattered throughout
the hilly areas of Northern New
Jersey.

NEW YORK, Nov. 20.-Stocks
were unable to hold their gains to-
day after early demand put the
market ahead.


Prices were mixed with slight
edge to the upside. Gains and
losses covered point range either
way.


Trading was active shortly after
the opening when the higher

a lull before selling commenced.


There was nothing like a run
away market at any time either
on the advance or when prices
started slipping.


Steels and rails stood out on

paratively greater weakness on

conda Copper, Eastman Kodak.

day at the near 20-year peak at
tanned Saturday when the Asso-
ciated Press average reached it's
best point since February 1881.

have made up their mind that this
Congress will do nothing that will
upset the even tenor of the Stock

against the excess profits tax

Because the three Allies could

But there would be difficulties

he said. The Americans had Of

In what may be the prelude to
another military withdrawal, the
French have begun removing
civilians by sea from Moncay.
Moncay is the important east
coast anchor of the North Indo-
China defense line.


There was no official indica-
ton, however, whether the French
would follow the pattern of seven
previous abandonments of from
tier posts and pull their troops
back after the civilians have gone.
The announcement said merely
the evacuation would tighten the
burden of the defending garrison.
The town already is under mortar
fire from Communicated Wet
Mini troops. -


Police today announced the
roundup of Is leaders of Wet
Mini terrorist organizations in
the Saigon area. They said they
discovered several large arms
caches.


Police in the past month have
arrested about 100 alleged Wet
Mimi terrorists here. They are
said to be members of q volunteer
suicide battalion. -
Nguyen Van Tam, chief of the
Wet Nam security forces, said ter
rorist activities have been reduced
in scale lately.


Wet Mini. pressure on Moncay
has been building up over the last
few daysZalong with probing at.
tacks al along the shaky l007rnile
defense line running from the east
coast anchor to Dinh Lap, western
terminal fortress.


Dinh Lap itself was being
threatened by strong concentra-

menaced the Dinh Lap commu1i-

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, June
1.-THE newspaper Berlingske
Tidende said last night American
troops will evacuate Greenland
starting June 80.


The foreign Office would not
comment on the report.


There have been frequent de-
mands here that the United
States give up the bases it estab-
lished during the war on the
Danish -owned Arctic island. They
were set up as weather stations,
communications posts, rescue units
and for operating forces.


When the Atlantic Pact was
negotiated in the spring of 1949
American officials said they
thought its defense provisions
would end Danish objections to
the United States installations
Such protests have continued
however.

ST. PAUL, Nebr., Nov. THE
body of Grover Cleveland Alex
ander lay today in a quiet ceme-
terry in the hills not far away from
this Central Nebraska town where
he was born.


Alexander, whose pitching wiz
ardry years ago elevated him
to baseball's Hall of Fame,
was buried yesterday with military
services conducted by the Ameri-
can Legion. He had served in the
AEF in World War I.


Earlier services in town were
conducted by retired minister.
the Rev. John Roe. Some 300
friends and fans attended.


The st. Louis Cardinals, for
whom "Old Pete" had once played,
paid for the funeral.


Alexander died here Saturday
of heart ailment.


One of those who came here
for the services was Alexander's
former wife, Aimee. She said the
500 a month which Alex had COL
lected after his playing days ended
came from Sam Breadon, late
president of the Cards. She said
the money was paid through Ma
tional League headquarters and
Alex always thought it was a PEN
sion from the league.


The only persons who knew the
actual source, she said, were her
self, Breadon, National League
President Ford Frick and Bill
Walsingham, Cardinals business
manager.


Walsingham later commented
from st. Louis that the pension
had been suggested by Breadon,
"but it came from National League
funds"

Mrs. Eli Stevens, 43, wife of Col
Stevens. State Department foreign
affairs specialist, was found dead
with a bullet wound in her head
in her apartment at the La Sale
Apartments. 1923 Connecticut
avenue NV. at 8 am. today.


A note in Mrs. Stevens hand
writing found near her body indi-
Gated she had ended her life be-
cause of dependency, homicide
squad detectives said.


Mrs. Stevens body, clad in a
nightgown. was found by her IA
year-old daughter. Myna, who had
been awakened by a telephone call
from her father. Beside the body
was a Mauser pistol with one
bullet fired, police said. They
added that Mrs. Stevens appar-
emily placed the gun in her mouth
before firing the fatal shot.


Police said Mrs. Stevens Suf-
fered a nervous breakdown about
three years ago and was separated
on a friendly basis from her hus-
band, retired Army colonel.


With her daughter, Mrs. Stevens
came to Washington from their
home in Houston. Tex, early this
month for a visit.


Col. Stevens told police he took
his wife and daughter for drive
last night and arranged to have
breakfast with them this morning.
Col. Stevens lives at the Army and
Navy Club. He told police his
wife did not seem respondent last
night, although she was unusually
quiet.


Col. Stevens called his wife's
apartment to keep their breakfast
date shortly before 8 am. His
daughter found her mothers body
as she hastened to answer the call.
Mrs. Stevens had been dead about
six hours, medical examiner
said.


Col. Stevens, who retired from
the Army in 1948. was appointed
to his State Department post last
November.

government spokesman said

PORTLAND. Oreg.. Oct. 30
Flooding Oregon rivers today
added death and destruction tc
the heavy toll already inflicted
on the Pacific Northwest from
five days of Pacific storms.


The floods had claimed two
lives and one person was missing
this morning after rivers, swoller
by the prolonged steady rain
went out of their banks all tn,
way from the Oregon coast to tn,
Cascade range. Scores of town
were isolated as highways werl
blocked and train schedules in
terrupted. Many rural familie!
were marooned and schools ane
lumber mills closed.


New areas were evacuated az
the crest of the rampaging Will
liamette River, major stream ir
the area, moved into the mid
Willamette valley.


Crest Passes Eugene.


The food crest passed Eugene
last night. where hundreds were
evacuated yesterday as lowlands
were indunated.


The upper Willamette, however
was falling almost as rapidly as il
had risen and some highways
closed by water yesterday. were
reopened.


At Eugene, where the river
crested last night at 15.9 feet
nearly feet above flood stage
the Willamette this morning had
dropped back near flood stage OF
IL feet.


Red Cross Provides Shelter.


Some observers there said it
was the fastest rise and fall of
any flood in memory. Damage
was not expected to. be extensive,
but the Red Cross provided shell
ter for about 1000 after the evac-
uation of many in rowboats.


The crest was expected here
Wednesday night.


Meantime, the Snake River, a
tributary of the vast Columbia,
rose 3 feet during the night at
Charleston, Idaho. But weather
bureau river forecasters here said
they expected no flooding on the
Snake or Columbia.


In Oregon's Umpqua River val
ley. about 1000 persons scurried to
higher ground yesterday to escape
the flood. Many were housed at
Roseburg, center of the area and
at nearby smaller communities.


Aid Rushed to Roseburg.


Roseburg's plight was declared
a flood emergency by the Red
Cross and supplies and staff aides
were rushed there from other
West Coast cities. The city of
Grants Pass was isolated.


Crescent City. Calf, was iso-
lated yesterday and passengers of
four buses and more than 100
cars were stranded there.


Highways in a vast area were
severed by bridge washouts, fallen
trees and land slides. Only one
main trunk route linked Oregon
and California. United States
80 and the coast high
way 101 were under water in a
dozen places.


The victims were Hollis Nc
Guire, 80, Placer, Oreg., who died
after being pulled from the debris
of a smashed bridge, and Mrs.
Leona Higgins, 81, who drowned
in the rampaging Coquille River
near the Oregon coast. Motorist
Lester Howe, Myrtle Point, was
in the same river after a
car plunged into the flooded
stream. His companion. Weber
Mast. was rescued.

Four Montgomery County police

thinking telephone operator noti-
fled them something was wrong
at the house.


Mrs Elizabeth Erner, who lived
alone in her home at TIA Ritchie
avenue, was carried unconscious
from her kitchen after the opera

from Mrs. Erner's phone.


Blocked from entering the front
of the house by flames, Sergt. Mel
vim Wheeler and Pvts. Eldridge
Pier. Charles Lauritzen and Rich
ard Sedgewick smashed in a
kitchen window and carried Mrs.
Erner to safety They found her
lying on the floor. overcome by
smoke.


Sergt. Wheeler said Mrs. Erner
apparently had been sleeping on
a living room couch when the
fire broke out and had gone to
the kitchen to call for help when
overcome.


She was taken to Washington
Sanitarium where her condition
today was reported as good.


The fire. apparently starting
from an explosion in an oil burner
in the basement, ignited trash
stored nearby and badly burned
the entire front of the two-story
frame house. Damage was esti-
mated at $4,000.

When at wars end, Selective Service Direc-
tor General Hershey strongly recommended that
the wages earned by the conscientious objectors
and paid into the Treasury should be appro-
priated for welfare fund for these men and
their families the conscientious objectors them
selves rejected the proposal. They voted instead
that the money, which amounts to s., 1927 ,641 81,
be turned over to CARE for furtherance of it's
program of restocking the war-ravaged Libraries
Of the world with the latest and best in scien-
tific and technical books and journals. The
crying need for such intellectual nourishment
in countries which suffered an almost ten-year
blackout of medical, scientific and professional
information need hardly be labored here. Nor
does it seem necessary to point out that the
advantages OF making self-help available to
professional men in other countries are mutual.


Yet this humanitarian gesture was slapped
down in the House on Wednesday. The measure
was defeated amid chorus OF unworthy full
limitations about economy, isolationism and
drearily familiar money down. -the-rathole"
formulas. Since the fund does not come out
OF tax money, the economy talk is not convinc-
ing. The contention that the program dupli-
Gates the work of the State Department Library
service was not well made, since CARE seeks
only to provide books for already established
national institutions, while the State Depart
ment must house, equip and staff its libraries.
The objections voiced to the conscientious OBJ
jectors themselves were simply irrelevant.
These men contributed total Of 8,237, 1856 man
days of labor during the national emergency.
They have, as Representative Judd, sponsor of the
bill, points out "a moral equity" in the funds
paid to those among them who were assigned
to private employers. They have chosen q
worthy purpose for their disposition.

Indiana, Illinois and Missouri.

ers. as well as smaller streams

areas. A new evacuation was
started by some 5000 persons
from the New Madrid fioodway
below Charleston, in Southeast
Missouri.


The rain belt extended from
Tennessee. Kentucky and Illinois
eastward to the Atlantic Coast.


Ice storms and snow dealt
damaging blows to wide areas
over the Midwest and in Southern
New York and Northern Penn
sylvania.


Power and telephone service In
hundreds of Midwest communities
was disrupted. Highway travel
was slowed by the glazed condi-
tions.


Temperatures, generally, over
the country were not severe.

The several French regiments

There are four main tradi-

ULM, Germany, Feb. 21.-When
Gestapo agents hanged two Mu-
Mich students in 1943 they unwit-
tingly helped found postwar Ger
many's most democratic educa-
tional experiment.


With the deaths Of anti-Nazi
Hans and Sophie Scholl, their sis
ter Inge decided to devote herself
to teaching the German to think
for himself.


It is q gigantic and sometimes
discouraging task. Germans for
centuries have developed follow
the-Ieader mentality. Reaction
still is the rule in this defeated
country.


Miss Scholl remembers with a
shudder the day the Gestapo took
Hans and Sophie away because
they dared publicly to oppose the
Nazi dictatorship. She was con-
vinced that Germany's ultimate
salvation lay within itself; that
Germans must learn to develop

tempt failed.


The final result Of the election

Baltic search, said American
planes have been instructed to
fly only over the sea. Search
flights over land are being made
by Swedish planes, Capt. Kiln
ger said. The sea search carries
some American planes near the
southern tip of Sweden where
the base is located)


The newspaper Aftonbladet said
American rescue planes had made
two flights over Karlskrona, Swe-
den's biggest naval base on the
Baltic. This area is out of bounds
for all foreign planes and Swedish
civilian aircraft.


The Swedish defense staff said
it had granted American rescue
planes only limited permission to
fly over the island of Gotland.

Officials in charge of the National Air Races
have shown good judgment in dropping the
dangerous closed-course speed contests from the
1850 race program. 1t was during these pylon-
grazing thrill spectaces that noted flyer
Bill Odom and two other persons were killed
last year. Public demands for an end of such
races were made not only in Cleveland but in
many parts of the country after the fatal Odom
flight.


The decision means the abolishment of a
long standing feature of the races the Thomp-
son Trophy dash. Back in the days when plane
speeds were far less than those of today the
Thompson Trophy race was safer and more
practicable. With the advent OF souped-up
high-speed military-type fighter craft, however
the dangers of closed-course racing have greatly
increased


The committees action does not mean the
death kneI of speed at the National Air Races
Jet planes and high-speed propeller-driv craft
will compete again this year, but they will not
have to bank around pylons marking circular
course. They will be flown over straightaway
courses, where accident risks are at minimum
The only closed-course races will be for small
planes that easily maneuverable. There Is
no reason to believe that the races this year will
be any less interesting or less popular than they
have been in the past.

Prince Baudouin. Socialists criti-

the capital. In Verviers, East
Belgium, streetcar workers struck,

Heinkel, who built some of Nazi
Germany's best war planes, has
this word of advice for Western
powers in their aerial planning
for European defense: "They had
better quit wasting their time and
money in rival, unco-ordinated
experiments in military aircraft by
individual countries. They should
centralize all their efforts under
one control and develop mass pro-
duction of one good model for
each type Of plane.


"All Allied nations then could
shift planes where needed, use a
central stockpile of spare parts.
And they could build a lot more
planes lot faster than with many
varied models"

Balenciaga. the Spanish. de-

If it weren't for modern farm
machinery, Old Man Weather
might well have Americans worry
ing about this years food pro-
duction prospects.


The Agriculture Department re-
ports that bad weather has de-
layed the spring planting season
two or three weeks in the north
ern two-thirds of the country.


In past decades of the horse
drawn plow and planter, such de-
lays often were serious. But high
speed tractors, multiple-plows and
planters now make it possible for
farmers to catch up quickly, espe-
cially by working around the
clock.


Many Crops Hampered.


Crops hampered so far by un-
favorable weather include wheat,
oats, barley, cotton, corn and soy
beans. The winter wheat crop
may be the smallest since 1943
and about 1876 million bushels
with farm value of nearly $400
million-below the departments
forecast of last December.


Winter wheat prospects declined
IA million bushels in April after
dropping off 1872 million bushels
between last December and
April /. Major losses were in
the Southern Great Plains, where
dry weather and an infeStation
of green bugs plagued the crop.


But a reserve of $50 million
bushels from past big crops as
sures ample wheat supplies to
meet indicated market demands.


Rigid Quotas Unlikely.


The poor outlook for winter
wheat and delays in seeding spring
wheat virtually assured farmers
that they will not be obliged to
produce the 1851 crop under rigid
market quotas designed to cur
tail production.


This may be the first year since
1943 that production of winter
and spring wheat combined. will
fall below a billion bushels. The
record was 1854 900. 900 in 1947.


Not only has dry weather in the
Great Plains, and wet, cool weather
in other areas hindered produc-
ton. Frosts in the South have
heavily damaged the peach crop.
The yield may be less than half
last year.


The effect of a poor crop year
could be more serious for farmers
than consumers, because big sup
plies stored under price supports
offer consumers protection against
