McALESTER, Okla, Mar. 18.-
The deputy warden at the State
Penitentiary here walked into a
punishment building where % in
corrigible prisoners were loose
and successfully bargained yes
terday for the lives of two guards
they had overpowered.


Warden C. P. Burford was in
vestigating the incident today
after the prisoners staged a one
hour riot in the prisons Little
Alcatraz" yesterday.


Little Alcatraz" is building
inside the walls used for solitary
confinement of incorrigibles kept
separated from the other 1850
prisoners.


Warden Burford said Deputy
Warden H. c. Mcleod entered the
building unarmed to bargain with
the prisoners.


Warden Burford gave this ver-
sion:


Only one prisoner is permitted
out of a cell at a time. When
Guard Joe Bales released one
prisoner, he was attacked and
overpowered. The prisoner, whose
name was not made public, took
the keys to the other cells and re-
leased the others.

attacked by the released prisoners

with tear gas guns. There was no
way for the prisoners to escape
from the buildings. Even the
guards are prisoners inside the
building with the only key kept
in the guard tower.

BERLIN. May 27.-With pomp
and fanfare reminiscent of the
Hitler era, East Germany's Com
munist youth brigades paid hon.
age today to Russia's war dead.
Western troops and West German
police patrolled the Western Sec

heralded Whitsuntide rallies
steamed into high gear.


There were a few minor Incl
dents here and there, but mainly
the city was calm and orderly.
Three East German police, armed
with old German army carbines,
abducted German from the
American sector during the noon
hour and fired on Western police
when they attempted pursuit.


That was the second such Incl
dent in "a hours. The first was
forestalled last night when Brit
ish sector police seized two alleged
Communist agents as they were
pushing a political refugee into
an East-bound elevated train.


But all the Eastern police were
not happy. Eight young conscripts
fed to the Western sectors, Allied
officials reported, making a total
OF IA such deSerters so far.

More than 5000 blue-shirted
youngsters of the Free German
Youth FDD stood stifay while
wreaths were laid at the foot of
a Soviet memorial made largely
of marble from Hitler's former
chancellory.


The ceremony was a highlight
in the three-day FDJ demonstra-
tion which will be climaxed here
tomorrow with a monster parade.


Today's tribute to the war dead
OF country which was once Ger

have already gathered here.

which also was used to attack the
Western Allies, was strictly a Ger

long driveway into the grounds.

WINNIPEG, Manitoba. May 16.
Hip booted volunteers and SOL
diers piled more and more sand
bags behind Winnipeg's sodden
levees today. hoping they would
still hold as the Red Rivers flood
crest surged through the greater
Winnipeg area.


Brig. Ronald Morton, flood con-
troll chief. warned "a catastrophe
could still happen" But early
today the Red and its two tribu-
taries, the Seine and Assiniboine.
had held steady for 80 hours at
SOL feet.


That was - feet above flood
stage for the district but repre-
sented a drop of one-tenth of a
foot from the 1850 hgih reported
Sunday.


Though the army had COM
pleted final plans for a rapid
clearing of the entire area If tor
rental rains should again raise
the river much higher, there ap-
peared some slackening in the
steady stream of women and chill
dren who have been leaving the
city.


$4,000 Have Left City.


Already an estimated 10000
have gone to safer villages and
towns north. east and west of
the city. They left in answer to
official appeals for voluntary
tightening of the load on the city's
overtaxed public utilities.


But where thousands had
crammed railway and bus sta
tions during the week end. only a
few hundred today were moving
to the safety of dry centers.


D. M. Stephens, deputy min
lister of natural resources for
Manitoba, said last night the
rivers crest was passing the me-
tropolis. He predicted the wa
tiers would start a gradual drop
at noon today if no complications
occurred.


However. Army flood control
authorities still warned that
tragedy of life or further loss of
property still is quite possible"
Heavy rains anywhere in the wa
tersheds of the three rivers. they
said, might quickly wipe out any
gains and send the streams surg
ing still higher.


ASsiniboine Rises Slightly.


The Assiniboine already was ris-
ing slightly miles west in Sas-
katchewan. but no serious trouble
was expected from this.


Meanwhile, weary, water soaked
workers on the soggy. strained
bikes continued their anxious la
Dor to bolster the protecting
earthworks. Even If the waters
slowly receded as expected, the
levees still might give way.


Experts said the Red and its
two tributaries would have to fall
feet at least before greater Win
nipeg's bikes could be called out
of danger.

not enter Communist China. but

with Red Chinese representatives
either in Burma. Thailand (Siam)
or Hong Kong. The Tibetan gov
ernment had notified Peiping of

their remote capital. But the Chi
neSe Communists had not replied

even though the Chinese Reds
have pledged themselves to "liber-
ate" Tibet. there has been no evi-
dence yet OF an attempt by the
Chinese to inf1ltrate the country.
Tibet has long been regarded as
strongly Communist.


But the Communists are re-
ported already to have cleared the
approaches to this remote land on
China's southern borders. The
threat is a matter of grave con-
cern to the Buddhist monks who
govern Tibet under the 15-year-
old Dalai Lama.


hinged by the highest noun
tains in the world, Tibet has been
isolated from modern world strug-
giles. But the Moscow press has
repeatedly declared that the coun-
try must be driven from its CEN
turies-old ways and into the
stream of world communism,

Shanghai if the Reds change their

still can be diverted back to the
Yangtze area any time within the
next two or three days, Capt. VAL
demar Nielsen said he thought the
chance of his ships going through
with the evacuation could be
written off."-AP.

Dixie have denied them.

away affair for Bing and the boys.

pay. The friend said Dixie was

pected to visit the ranch later.

The prediction that velvet will
have a prominent place in the
spring and summer fashion pic

Pauline Trigere, New York fashion
designer.


Miss Trigere, who was the guest
at luncheon meeting Ct the
Washington Fashion Group, also
prophesied that another popular
item will be the short hip-length
straight linen square coat de-
signed to go over practically every
type of dress in the spring and
summer wardrobe.


Known as a trend setter, Miss
Trigere, who won the American
Fashion Critics award for 1949
displayed several creations from
her own collection at the lunch
con, which was held at the Wash
ington Hotel.


Featured in the group shown
yesterday were the short sleeved
coat and the sheer coat which
Miss Trigere introduced two years
ago and which she feels will be
important for day and evening
wear in the months TO come.


Special interest centered in a
full length black coat of taffeta
which had velvet trim on its short
sleeves.


The designer declared that large
black hats of velvet-usually asso-
ciated with winter wear - will
complete many spring and sum-
mer outfits this year.


Miss Trigere, whose appearance
at the luncheon yesterday was her
first in Washington, is French by
birth but has been in this country
since 1887.


Noted for her lack of fashion
eccentricities. she believes that
functionalism can exist in the
most high-style design.


Mrs. Alfred Pasternak and Mrs
Mary Jane Edwards also spoke at
the luncheon, describing imports
they had purchased in Paris re-

special guests who included Mrs.
Harold H. Burton and Mrs. M.
Robert Guggenheim.

charge of the program.

BIRMINGHAM. Ala. Dec. %.
"A bomb last night heavily
damaged a dwelling occupied by
Negroes in a residential area pre-
viously zoned for white persons.


The bombing. the first here
since April 13. followed a ruling
of the United States Circuit
Court of Appeals against Bir-
mingham's racial zoning laws.


The dwelling was occupied by
Mrs. Mary Leans Monk, who had
led the court fight against resi-
Dental segregation here. Mrs.
Monk and five other occupants
Of the recently completed resi-
dence were unhurt.


The explosion tore away half
Of a bedroom wall. Mrs. Monk had
just left the room when the blast
took place. Police began an i'm
mediate investigation.


The bombing of Negro homes
here has occurred intermittently
since the late summer of 1947.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico, Feb
1.-Two Russian fishing vessels
heavily equipped with radio ane
radar devices, have entered waters
where the United States plans
its largest postwar. maneuvers.


They are the 328-ton sister
schooners Kometa and Osminoe
and are similar to ships which
visited the Caribbean area last
year when the United States Navy
was staging smaller but important
maneuvers.


The schooners arrived at ST
Thomas. Virgin Islands, last Sun.
day and sailed for Panama Tues
day.


Their tightlipped officers said
they were bound for Panama, but
natives said they had heard the
Russians mention Vladivostok,
The vessels were built in Finland
as war reparations.


Admiral Daniel E. Barley, COM
mandant of the 10th Naval Dis
trict with headquarters here, said
the situation is we'll In hand


Two other Russian fishing
vessels" docked at Honolulu Mon
day. They were described as be-
ing of the same type that showed
up just before the 1948 atomic
tests at Eniwetok. More atomic
tests are scheduled for this year
at the Eniwetok Island proving

Carbon monoxide fumes that
seeped into their automobile
through the partly opened rear
trunk today were blamed for the
deaths of a Montgomery County
couple and a Virginia youth near
Harrisonburg, Va, yesterday.


Cecil Thacker. %, and his wife,
Anna Thacker, 27. of Great Falls
road near Potomac, Md, and
Bobby Delaney. 18, of Grundy,
Buchanan County, Va, were
found dead in Mr.. Thacker's car
on Route II just north of Har-
Irisonburg.


Virginia State police said the
car was parked beside the road
and that the motor was running.
A small white dog was dead in
the rear trunk. Police said the
trunk had been left ajar about
three inches, apparently to pro-
vide air for the dog. A strong
wind, however, must have blown
the deadly carbon monoxide fumes
into the car through the partly
opened trunk, police said. The
fumes might have been seeping
into the car while it was moving,
causing Mr.. Thacker to become
drowsy and pull off the road to
sleep, police added.


Police said the Tllackers were
returning to their home near Po-
tomac after spending the week end
with Mrs. Thacker's sister near
Grundy. They were bringing the
Delaney youth with them.


Mr.. Thacker worked as a truck
driver for the National Park
Service. A brother, Elmer Thacker.
left Potomac yesterday to 60 to
Harrisonburg to make funeral ar
lrangements. The bodies were
taken to Loving's funeral home at
Harrisonburg.


Police said they believed the
Delaney youth also worked in the
Washington area, but did not
have any address for him except
'Grundy, Va.

A new automatic pilot being
produced for the Air Force can
guide jet planes through good
or bad weather and may even
fire their guns aimed by radar.


The Air Force announced the
device yesterday, calling it "the
first mechanism developed which
can meet the high speed and
maneuverability required to fly
today's jet fighters. Automatic
pilots are customary in bombers
and transports, but not fighters.


The new pilot, called the F-5
autopilot, was developed by Lear,
Inc. OF Grand Rapids, Mich, in
cooperation with the Air Materiel
Command.


Once off the ground. the pilot
can point his plane toward its
goal and relax. To turn right or
left, to climb or descend, he needs
only two tiny controls to per-
form all simple flying maneuvers

jib sheet, centerboard and other
chores while his skipper bellows
and takes the tiller-is being re-
membered this week end by Cam
bridge Yacht Club.


Club officials have announced
first, second and third place series
prizes for both skipper and crew
in the clubs annual regatta open
ing here tomorrow morning.


Clubs rarely award trophies to
anyone but shippers of winning
boats. But Cambridge said it
wanted to add crews "in recog-
milton of the indispensable role
played by the crew."


Races are planned for Stars,
ThistleS, Indian Landing 20s,
Hamptons. Lightnings and Pen
gums.


Two races Tor each class will
be sailed tomorrow morning and
afternoon and the windup race
Sunday morning. Prizes will be
awarded early enough to permit
out-o of-town shippers to get on
the road for home.


The club will sponsor a crab
feast tomorrow night.
One of the week ends high
lights is a rowing race among the
younger generation around Cam
bridge. They compete in little
homemade affairs that resemble
bait box. >


Shippers are expected from as
far distant as Washington and
Norfolk.

FRANKFURT, Mar. 1.-THE
Western Allies are discussing an
American plan to let Germany
build ships of unlimited size and
speed for sale to other countries,
highly placed authorities disclosed
today.


THE Germans can sell $50
million worth of ships a year if
present Allied restrictions are
modified" these informants said.


The Petersburg agreement
among America, Britain and
France forbids the West Germans
to build ships over 1900 tons or
II knots in speed for either their
own use or for export.


The American plan would per-
NIT the Germans to build bigger
ships for export but would pro-
hibit them from using the ships
themselves, the sources said.


American, British and French
experts discussed the American
plan at a recent meeting, the in
formants said. They could not
say if the United States has for
mally submitted the plan to
Britain and France or whether
Anglo French sentiments were
simply sounded out there.


Officials said the American plan
has the double-barrelled aim of
providing jobs and of spurring
West Germany's tagging economy.

in most other commodities.

cities. Wholesalers here ascribed
the rise to seasonal scarcitieS.

also was counted as a main factor.


One chain here which raised
meat prices last week dropped
most of them back this week to
the earlier level. A spokesman
indicated this reflected only the
chains own policies, rather than
the overall market picture.

PEARL HARBOR, July l.
American military authorities be-
lieve Hawaii's defenses are ade-
ouate to fight off another Pearl
Harbor attack.


American officers concede that
ground. sea and air forces are low
IN number. But they feel that,
under the present situation" the
forces are sufficient.


They said magic-eye radar COM
pletely screens Hawaii on all
sides-although radar would not
necessarily give enough advance
warning to prevent an air attack
such as the December 7. 1941,
japanese raid.


Land Forces Total 1000.


Army, Air Force and Navy Off
GERS described military strength
In Hawaii like this:


Land forces - Total strength
about 1000, principally the Army'S
5th Regimental Combat. Team
at Schofield Barracks. The 5th
has about 1000 fully trained and
equipped troops. both infantry
and artillery. 1t was the last unit
to leave Korea when the Amer
ican occupation ended last year.


Sea forces-Except for "a few
patrol vessels" the Hawaiian Sea
Frontier has only those forces
which are in transit. Included in
that category at present are a
heavy cruiser, an escort carrier
and four deStroyers. A new task
force to back up the 7th Fleet
assigned to Gen. MacArthur-is
expected to be based here shortly.
Air Force Lacks Combat Planes.


Air-A variable number of
fighter planes and patrol craft.
The Air Force itself has no COM
bat planes here. The Navy has
two patrol squadrons and a train
ing group which can put fighters
into the air. The Air National
Guard has about 80 fighters.
There are no Jets.


Col. Robert N. Young, chief of
staff of the Army's Pacific forces,
and Col. Kendall j. Fielder, who
will relieve Col. Young July 20.
told an interviewer defenses are
considered adequate at the pres
ent time.


They and naval officers said
bases in Japan, Guam, the Philip
pines, the Marshalls and Alaska
probably would intercept attack
ers long before they reached Ha-
waii.


What about an atomic bombing?
Col. Fielder said:


Except for Pearl Harbor, if it
were full of ships. we don't have
anything here worth atom bomb
ing. Hawaii is not a suitable tar
get for an atom bomb"

and smiled broadly.


Annette smiled, too, but more
self-consciously. Emile looked
solemn, Cecile gulped when she
saw the crowd outside and Marie
looked almost frightened.


Or maybe the solemn one was
Cecile. And wasn't the one with
the prettiest smile Annette?


Nobody was sure, not even their
host, Francis Cardinal Spellman,
archbishop of New York.


The important thing was that
all five of the Dionne quintuplets
were holding up we'll under the
strain of hoodlights, popping flash
bulbs and the pushing, curious

quints thought of New York, they

derful" and they were every
happy" to be here. 1t was their
second venture into the United
States. The first was in 1943
when they went to launch some
ships in Wisconsin.

The quints came this time by
train from Corbeil, Ontario.


They peered curiously through
train windows while they waited
for policemen, policewomen and
priests to make room on the plat
form so they could get through
the crowd.

Dionne, a slight, dapper man who
has fathered nine other children,

pressed by the reception.

the quints. came along, with sew
eral teachers, a nurse and a few
Dionne friends.


The quints stepped smartly-in
their first high-heeled shoes. it
was said-up the platform and
into Grand Central Station where

The quintS' first look at the city
was a quick one-across town in
Ia bus. through Times Square, up
Broadway to Central Park, and
then to a convent where they will
stay during their four-day visit.


They were tired, but were sure
to be more tired after today's
events, which include a rehearsal
for their singing appearance at

beautician, more sightseeing, and
then the dinner,

Graveside services were held to-
day in Mount Olivet Cemetery for
Mrs. Mary Brooks, 115-year -old
ex-slave whose sight was restored
after an operation last month in
Gallinger Hospital.


Mrs. Brooks, who had been to-
tally blind for more than 30 years,
was able. after the surgery, to rec
ognize friends, objects and color.


She died Monday at the Little
Sisters of the Poor Home, where
she had been living since 1912.


On her last birthday Mrs.
Brooks told reporters she was
born in Prince Georges County.
Md, where her father was a
slave. She didn't remember when
she was born. but sisters at the
home list her birth date as Decem-
ber %. 1884.


When the aged colored woman
was taken to Gallinger Hospital
a few months ago for treatment
of the arteries of her legs, the
Sisters asked If anything could
be done about her eyes.


Doctors removed the lens from
her right eye. which had formed
an Opaque cataract. Gradually
her sight returned.


Mrs. Brooks had no survivors.

Ralph Bogart. the first Middle

Miss Elizabeth (Sister) Kenny,
still crusading after 40 years, be-

Of the cause of polio, which has
kept her at bitter odds with doc

The Australian-born nurse, who
has won worldwide acclaim for
her work with polio victims, gave
the scientific data yesterday to
Representative Judd. Republican,
of Minnesota, himself a physician.


Sister Kenny has never claimed
she could cure polio. But she in
sists her techniques of treatment
can prevent many of the crippling
defects the disease causes.


Techniques Adopted.


Indeed, most doctors have
adopted many of her principles
and techniques. What they OBJ
ject to is her iron-clad insistence
that her methods be followed to
the letter and that treatment be
given only by people trained under
her supervision.


But at the base of the con-
troversy is Sister Kenny's concept
that the virus that causes polio
can settle in any part of the body,
exclusive of the nervous system.
Most doctors believe the polio
virus initially attacks the nervous
system-the brain and spinal cord
and that crippling effects result
from this damage.


The large, white-haired nurse
told reporters the data she gave
DR.. Judd proved by microphoto-
graphs that the virus has been
found in muscles and tissues ly-
ing close to the skin and in inter-
nal organs. Removed from these
infections, she said, the virus
transmitted polio to monkeys.
Years Of Research.
These results, she said, came
from years of research at New
York's Columbia Hospital, the
Cajal Institute in Madrid and the
Neurological Institute in Brussels


She gave them to DR.. Judd, she
said, for transmission to the pre-
mier of Queensland, Australia, as
an official report of the work she
has done since coming to this
country as IAN official visitor On
a mission" 10 years ago.


In her talk with reporters, Sis
ter Kenny at time lashed out at
the medical profession, criticizing
particularly the National Founda-

refusing to go along with her
teachings.


Evidence Lacking Before.

said, was lacking before.

basic concept she proposes, Sister

impossible. She showed X-rays,
which, she said, showed damage
had been done to muscles treated
with other methods.

Many of us have heard about the
cleverness of spiders, especially the
balloonists, suspension bridge build
ers, crafty snare settlers, skillful
hinge-door constructors and diving
bell makers, but few have ever
watched them fish for top minnows
or catfish.


Many of the best anglers belong
to the Dolomedes tribe, known
through the South and from New
England to Texas. Wherever there
are streams or marshy places, you
will discover these poachers sneak
ing through the grass along the
edges of the watery places.


They are exceptionally handsome
spiders of goodly size, dressed in
greenish-gray fur coats with a mar
row white ribbon band extending
around the entire body. On the
underside you will find six tiny
white buttons and six dark spots on
she sterumn. They are harmless
and very easily frightened, to get
elt of your way they plunge into
the water below, always attached to
a heavy silk rope by which they
climb back to safety.


Hanging over the water, anchored
to a sturdy weed stem, the fisher
man is watching the water for top
minnows or baby catfish. Though
provided with four eyes, vision is
poor. Yet, I have never seen the
fisherman fail to spot a swarm of
small black catfish trailing their
devoted father. The catfish babies
thrust their ugly broad heads above
the surface, their jaws work furi-
ously, hoping for small food particles


Suddenly the fisherman drops
upon small catfish. Both go under,
but the hairs on the spiders body
trap the air so that air bubbles buoy
the spider and victim quickly to the
surface. The fish thraShes madly
to get free, the spider sinks his jaws
more deeply into his skull while his
two hind legs hold fast to the pro-
testing victim.


. In between struggles, the fisher
man n1bbleS on the captive's head.
AT last the poor fish gives up. The
fisherman cautiously releases the
grip of his legs, but holds faster with
his jaws. With the hind legs free,
the victor paddles his catch toward
IA cluster of weed stems strong
enough to bear the weight of fisher
man and catch. Here the angler
enjoys his fresh fish before dropping
the carcass back into the water.


Mother Dolomedes constructs a
gray silk egg purse the size of a
small red cherry, large enough to
hold up to BIT eggs. She fastens
her egg basket to her body with
strong cables dragging it with her
for months.


She fastens it among some shrub
leaves, which she sews together
then strews the area with silken
strands, the nursery for her babies.
No food is brought to them, follow
ing the custom of their tribe the
stronger eat the weaker. The
youngsters are soon poaching on
tiny creatures that abound in the
water below their, nursery, and
within a short time they are as
expert at angling as their long
legged father.

Thieves took nearly $4,000 from
safe in the Super-Freez Market
at 725 Eleventh street NV, dur
ing the week end after first
breaking into the Button Shop
next door. police were told today


Maurice Rosenfield, proprietor
Of the market. told police he was
sure he had locked the safe when
he left Saturday and he was the
only one who knew the combina-
tion.


The safe was not forced. Police
said, however, that opening it via
the combination was not too diff
cult for a housebreaker with safe
knowledge.


Safe Relocked by Thieves.
Mr.. Rosenfield said the thieves
locked the safe behind them after
removing its contents.


The thieves, he said, apparently
climbed from the roof into the
third floor of the building hous-
ing the Button Shop. They made
their way to the first floor but
the Button Shop reported nothing
missing.


Mr.. Rosenfield figured they then
discovered their mistake, climbed
back to the roof and broke into
his building by shattering sky
light over bathroom. He said
they crashed through bolteo
door to the combination Office and
meat-chopping room, where the
safe was located.


Checks Left on Chopping Block.


After looting the safe, the
thieves left the building by TAX
ing a ladder to the third floor
bathroom and climbing through
the broken skylight, he said.


Police had two clues. On the
meat chopping-block, the thieves
left three checks which police
planned to test for fingerprints
In the basement were footprints
in the sawdust. Police theorizec
the thieves explored the base
ment for an exit before taking tt
the roof. Molds were being made
OF the footprints.


MIR. Rosenfield said the stolen
cash represented his Friday ano
Saturday receipts.

A new dispute developed be-
tween Falls Church and Fairfax
County yesterday as both juris-
dictionS started billing about 100
county residents for sewer service.


Residents of Walnut Hills, Tim
ber Lane and Poplar Heights sec
tions of the county. who custo-
marily have paid sewer bills to
Falls Church, yesterday got bills
from Fairfax County. Most said
they already have paid the city
for sewer service during the period
for which the county seeks to
collect.


Lien Power Emphasized.


The Fairfax bills, of Sc for three
months, bear stern reminder
that the law permits the county
to enforce liens against properties
involved if bills are not paid by
July 81.
Fairfax County Sanitary Engi-
neer James ]. Corbalis, jr., said
all residents who started receiving
bills from the county yesterday
live in areas sought for annexa-
ton by Falls Church.


Mr.. Corbalis said sewers that
serve the affected homes were
built by private developers, feed
into the city sewage system and
then flow into the county-con-
trolled Holmes Run trunk sewer,
as does most sewage from within
Falls Church. The Sanitary engi-
neer said the city has been billing
the 100 county residents although
the county is responsible for main
tanning their sewers.


According to Mr.. Corbalis, the
county had tried to reach an
agreement with the city so that
Fairfax would make payments to
the city for the portion of the city
sewer that serves the homes, and
Falls Church in turn would pay
the county for emptying the sew
age into the county controlled
facility. Mr.. Corbalis said Falls
Church had been unwilling to
make any agreement while its
annexation suit against the county
is pending.


County Rate Is Lower.


The county sewer service rate
of So month is a few cents lower
than the city rate. Residents Of
the three subdivisions also pay
water bills to the city, which sup
plies their water.


Observers expect the issue will
wind up in court, where two other
disputes between city and county
are pending. One is annexation
and the other involves how much
debt the city should have assumed
from the county when Falls
Church became an independent
body.

Eight thousand sea otters live in
colonies along the coasts of Alaska
and the Aleutian Islands. They are
all that remains after millions were
slaughtered by the Russian and
American fur traders. At one time
sea otterS were found all along the
Pacific coast and small-scale wars
were waged over the herds.


The Russians were the first
Europeans to discover sea otters and
were quick to realize the value of
their beautiful warm fur. The small
sea animals, not over IL inches
long, wear lustrous, deep, brown fur
frosted in white. The round head
and throat are yellowish or grayish
white. Each pelt was worth more
than a score of common skins to the
traders.

be foolish to eliminate animals pro-

rapacious hunters drove them to the

for the natives who only took what
they needed. From the day in 1741
when Bering and his crew first saw

halted. With the passage of time

The Yankees today had slipped
to third place in the torrid Amer
lean League race and the Tigers,
safe in front for the moment with
a 22-game lead, now must con-
tend with the onrushing Indians.


The Yankees. confident of TAX
ing over first place during their
three-game series with the Tigers
that ended yesterday. were de-
cisively beaten in all three games.


Young Art Houtteman, ace of

terday. to 2. Dizzy Trout and
Hal White turned back the Yanks
in the other two games.


AS result the Tigers, who were

the Yanks to third, 31a games off
the pace. The Indians, tied with
the Yanks for second place yes
terday but who did not play, thus
moved past New York into second

The Tigers. like a good many

look upon Cleveland as the team
to beat in the league race.


Yanks Are Stopped.


The Tigers entered the New
York series with a crippled pitch
ing staff. but swept the series
convincingly. In the 27 innings of
the three games, the Tigers made
16 runs on 27 hits while holding
the Yanks to 5 runs on IA hits.


In addition, the Tiger pitchers
stopped the Yankee big guns cold.


Joe Di Maggie got only two
singles in II times at bat and
failed to score or bat in run.
Yogi Berra got four hits in 10, but
scored only one run and failed to
bat any across.


Johnny Mize, who hit two hon.
ers, got three hits in IL tries. He
scored one other run in addition
to his homers and batted in two
more in addition to those pro-
duced by his round trippers. In
all, he either scored or batted in
four of the five runs the Yanks
scored in the series.


Wertz Has Big Series.


On the other hand, Vic Wertz.
Tiger outfield star who is in the
midst of a batting spree, had four
hits in six times at bat. scored
three runs, had two homers and
batted in three other runs.


Four runs in the first inning
tucked yesterdays game away for
Detroit. Ed Lopat. shooting for
his 14th win, got only one man out.


The 31,713 spectators hardly
had settled in their seats before
the Tigers had the game on ice.


The Yanks failed to score in
the top of the first and when
Detroit came to bat, the lead-off
man, Johnny Lipon, singled.
Jerry Priddy walked. Lopat
gummed up George Kell's bunt to
fill the bases and Wertz crashed
a double to right center, scoring |
two runs. Hoot Evers fouled out,
but Kell tailed from third after |
the catch when Second Baseman |
Jerry Coleman caught the ball
over his shoulder down the right
field line. Don Kolloway's single |
scored Wertz.


Fred Sanford and Joe Page held
the Tigers hitless until the eighth
and Mize narrowed New York's
deficit to AZ with a home run in
the fourth after Hank Bauer had
walked.


Houtteman scattered three sin
giles after that blow. though, and
the Tigers gave him added insur-
ance in the eighth when Kell
doubled, Wertz sacrificed and
Evers flied deep to left, scoring
Kell.


1t was the 18th victory for Hout-
teman.


Carrasquel Hits Again.


The only other action in the
American League had nothing to
do with the pennant race as sixth
place Chicago shut out seventh
place Philadelphia, 10.


Chico Carrasquel, the White
Sox' fine young shortstop,
stretched his consecutive game
hitting streak to % with a sixth
inning single.


The four other clubs in the
American were not scheduled.


Rain slaslfed the National
League schedule, washing out a
Observation-Disclosures day game
and a Cincinnati-at-P Philadelphia
night game. Chicago and New
York were not scheduled.


Vern Bickford, the Braves bril-
liant highlander. came up with
his second straight four-hitter
for 81 victory over the Cardi-
mails. The triumph boosted the
Braves into second place in front
of the idle Dodgers. The Braves
now are three games back of the
leading Phillies.


One of the most important
series in the National League race
opens tonight at Philadelphia,
with the Phils against the Cardi-

react to their situation in char
acteristic fashion. Some will hide

sent It: some will suffer keenly:

home unity In their behavior.

ing necessity to endure in silence.

thetic ears they find much-needed

saying little, but sending out af-
fectionate sympathetic feeling

truth and help him face a hard
fact: nobody lives alone; every

BERLIN, Sept. East Ger
many's Communist rulers rocked
their party and government today
with a startling purge of highly

Six party members, including a

thrown out of the Socialist Unity
(Communistl Party, the official

land announced.


-Four more were elected from

More expulsions were predicted.


The party newspaper gave two

with American spies" and exhib-
iting Russian feeling"


Those elected from the party
were:


Paul Merker, state secretary in
the Agriculture Ministry and
Politburo member until the re-
organization of the Socialist Unity
Party in July.


Leo Bauer, chief editor of
Radio Berlin:


Bruno Goldhammer, deputy to
Propaganda Chief Gerhard Eisler;


Will Kreikemeyer, general di-
rector of the Soviet Zone rail-
way system.


Lex Ende, former chief editor
of Neues Deutschland and later
editor of the Communist Friend
enspost.


Maria Weiterer, an unidentified
party member.


Without party status, none of
them can hope to retain their
state jobs. Bauer Is known to
have been thrown out of the
radio station already. Goldham-
n1er has not been seen in Eisler's
Office recently.


The purge action, Neues
Deutschland said, was taken by
the party Politburo at the direc-
ton of Party Secretary General
Walter Ulbricht, named to that
post five weeks ago. The same
party post in Russia, provided
Joseph Stain with his spring.
board to power.


Neues Deutschland admitted
the German Communist Party's
ranks are corroded with members
who no longer can obey Russian
dictates without question. This
is the worst sin that can be
charged against a Communist.


Deprived of their government
Jobs but still retained as party
members were Wolfgang Lang
hoff, manager of East Berlin's
Deutschen Theater, and Bruno
Fuhrmann, Hans Teubner and
Walter Beling, all of whom held
minor state positions.


10 Charged as Spies.


The general charge of espionage
was leveled at all 10 purgees. In
addition they were accused of
lacking confidence in the Soviet
Union.


NeueS Deutschland said there
was evidence they had been in
touch with the. American Office
of Strategic Services during the
war. They we're also said to have
associated with Noel H. Field,
former American State Depart
ment erhploye who disappeared
mysteriously behind the iron cur
tain in May, 1949.


The Communists said recently
that Mr.. Field was an American
spy but did not disclose what had
happened to him.


The purge has great historical
significance" Neues Deutschland
asserted.


''It is no exaggeration to say
that it marks the beginning of
a new stage in the history of our
party" the paper declared.


Probe Continues.


NeueS Deutschland said that in
quiry into the purgee's contacts
with Mr.. Field was continuing.
1t added:


"It must be assumed this will
contribute to further clearing and
cleaning of the party of enemy
agents and hampering elements. :"


Most of those named were refu-
gees from Hitler's Reich. AS
fighters against fascism they sup
piled Allied agents in Switzerland
with information and help during
the war. The party organ indi-
Gated they had retained Western
ideas repugnant to the Commu-
nists.


Merker and Goldhammer had
been pro-Communist for more
than 20 years. The latter was
bounded by the Nazis through a
half dozen concentration camps
until he escaped half dead and hid
in Northern Italy on the Swiss
border. Veteran correspondents
who had known him well were
surprised at the charge of dis
loyalty to the party.

NEW YORK, Nov. lit ap-
pears certain today that the par.
tial coast-to-coast telephone strike
will continue over the week end.
1t now is in its third day.


The first Federal peace talks
failed yesterday after only one OF
several pay and contract issues
was discussed. No new joint ses-
sion was planned before tomorrow
afternoon.


At the same time. the striking
C1O Communications Workers of
America started a new system of
"hit-and-run" picketing aimed at
causing the greatest possible con-
fusion in the huge Bell system.


Strike Efforts Are Spotty.


1t was designed to keep the
company from mobilizing clerks
and supervisors fast enough to
handle the struck jobs at any one
place.


The national effect of the strike
was spotty and varied widely from
city to city. The greatest sufferers
were the long distance service and
areas with manual telephone ex-
changes-both requiring direct
operators.


Automatic dial service, which
includes about 10 per cent of the
Nations phones, was not affected
at once. If the strike lasts long
enough, however, wear and tear
and breakdowns could cut into the
dial system. The maintenance
men of Bells subsidiary Western
Electric Co.. responsible for IN
stallation and repair. are the prin-
cipal CWA division on strike.


The union said yesterday that
of its nearly 100000 members,
$4,000 were actually on strike and
another $1,000 were honoring the
picket lines-a total of 10000
out of work.


The company estimated that
two-thirds of its national service
was normal, and the remainder
spotty. CWA divisions are striking
in all but five New England states.


The main quarrel is a 13-month
dispute between Western Electric
and CWA's maintenance Division
6 and Distributing Division Is.


Pay and Contract Are Issues.


The two principal issues are pay
rate and contract duration. The
union says it has asked for Sub
stantially" higher wage without
revealing publicly any exact
amount. However, a source close
to the situation says that Division
6. main union involved. has asked
for a 15-cents-an-hour increase
while Western Electric has offered
11A cents. Present pay rates
range from $1.55 to $1.62 an hour.


The union has asked for a one
year agreement while the COM
pany has demanded a 16-months
contract.


In yesterdays mediation talks,
Federal Conciliator Walter Mag
giolo said both sides were still
deadlocked over the contract
duration-the only issue discussed.
He planned separate talks with
the parties today, with new joint
session tomorrow.


The first violence in the dispute
came at Philadelphia, where police
formed flying wedge to clear the
way for trucks that pickets had
tried to barricade at two ware
houses. Division 18 charges the
police with strike-breaking activi-
ties, but police said they were only
maintaining order.


At Springfield. Mo-. 3-inch
cable containing $50 pairs OF
wires was cut with an ak, South

Bell reported main cable was

PENNSYLVANIA Station were blanked
out after their mouthpiece dia-
phragms were removed. others
were ripped from booths in tav-
erns and stores near the Western

1--WE have only three or four

satisfied with the Navy material,

it against outside opposition.


"I'll be lucky if we can field a

Frank Attorney. were hurt. Three

up before they couldn't even start.


Schedule Toning Is Hinted.

take now after trying three
coaches in four seasons is prob
lematical.


Miller went around mumbling
about really going after players.
Capt. Howard Caldwell observed
that next Saturday it's Prince
ton, and that's more in our
league"


Did that mean Navy would
tone down its schedule, which
now includes the best represen-
tatives from all sections of the
country?


Gould be, could be-" said Capt.
Caldwell thoughtfully.

money with which to tackle the job which Con-

that the Slum Clearance and Redevelopment Act
was passed-minus any appropriation For four
years the Redevelopment Land Agency has
struggled along without even the few dollars
needed to buy stationery or other office supplies.


Now all has changed. In fact the situation
has changed so completely that today the agency
finds itself with $2.2 million and no immediate
project on which to spend it. The money has
been allocated from Federal housing funds by
the Housing and Home Finance Agency, under
specific authority written into the Federal Hous-
ing Act. The grant is contingent on the adoption
within reasonable time of an approved plan
for redeveloping a slum section. The District
Commissioners, the National Capital Park and
Planning Commission and the Redevelopment
Land Agency once had what looked like good
plan, but 1t has gone out the window. This was
the program to rebuild Marshall Heights in the
eastern corner of the District. The residents of
that unplanned area objected so strenuously to
the proposal that Congress ordered it abandoned.


Now the planners must start all over again.
Their sad experience with Marshall Heights has
caused misgivngs about undertaking similar
projects elsewhere. They have learned the i'm
portance of obtaining the full cooperation of
the community slated for improvement. That
this is not an easy task has been proved by
what happened at Marshall Heights. For this
reason they are not apt to rush into another
project without careful consideration of all
angles-including that of public relations. Once
a feasible plan is adopted, however, Washingtons
long g-delayed slum-cearance program should be
able to start moving.

NEW YORK, Mar. New
York City has clamped strict, new
rules on the sale of theater tickets.


The tighter supervision was
imposed yesterday following a
lengthy ticket-scalping investiga-
ton during which "a ticket agen-
cies were closed for overcharging
or other offenses.


The new regulations require
ticket brokers to keep detailed
records on all sales, and forbid
charging any premium or bonus
above the standard 75-cent-a-
ticket brokers' fee.


Exchanges of tickets between
brokers are limited under the new
rules, to prevent one broker from
cornering a large block of tickets
for any particular show.
Violators may lose their licenses.


The probe into theater ticket
sales was ordered by Mayor Will
liam O'Dwyer after reports that
tickets to hit shows were selling
as high as $50 apiece.

BERN, Switzerland, Feb. 25.-A
Swiss military court today con-
victed Willy Gerber, Al, a Swiss
Army mechanic, of being a paid
spy for six nations, including the
United States, and sentenced him
to 20 years Imprisonment.


Gerber told the court he had
supplied information about Ger
man and Italian war activities to
the United States from 1912 to
1945 but asserted he received no
pay for the work.


Maj. M. Real, the prosecutor,
commented in reply:


1T seems highly improbable
that Gerber took no money from
the Americans. That would con-
tradict not only his pronounced
greed and avarice, but also the
business mentality of the Ameri-
cans"


Pleaded Guilty.


Gerber had pleaded guilty to a
long list of charges, including
treason and systematic military,
economic and political espionage
in Switzerland for Britain, France
and the United States since 1887,
as well as stealing top secret plans
and documents from the Swiss
army. He also was accused of spy
ing against Germany and Italy
for the Allies during the war. In
addition, the prosecution said, he
supplied information to Sweden,
Turkey and Yugoslavia as side
line.


His 3-day trial was conducted
for the most part in secret. During
a brief public session last night,
Maj. Real. demanded the maxi
mum penalty-life imprisonment.


During the war" he declared.
"two men were sentenced to death
and executed because they be-
trayed some munition depots and
mine positions. Compared with
these men, Gerber betrayed hun
dred times more"


Switzerland has no death PEN
atty in peacetime.


Money Confiscated.


The sentence included confisca-
tion of $7,150 from $4,000 bank
account Gerber had in New York.
The account was taken over by
the Swiss when Gerber was ar
rested last July. Maj. Real said
the money represented the amount
Gerber was known to have taken
from British and French diplo-
mats in Switzerland for espionage
activities, but added his actual
earnings were much higher.

BONN, Germany, April 24.-Re-
lations between the seven months
old West German republic and
its Western Allied sponsors will
undergo severe test this week.


There is tension between the
Bonn regime and the Allied high
commission over both domestic
and foreign issues.


Even as Chancellor Konrad
Adenauer was asking for more
powers for his republic, the high
commission vetoed two pieces of
domestic legislation concerning
taxation and reform of the civil
service.


The vetoes, which are provis-
ional, will be discussed by Allied
and German experts this week.
DR.. Adenauer hopes for a final de-
cision when he meets with the
high commissioners here Thurs
day.


The Allied high commission We
toed an income tax cut because
1t felt the slash might increase
need for foreign aid and swell
West Germany's federal deficit. A
law for reform of the civil service
was diSapproved because the COM
mission felt it failed to carry out
wishes that the traditionally au-
thoritarian service should be made
more democratic.


Chief topic in the foreign field
is whether Western Germany will
accept the invitation to join the
consultative council of the Euro
pean assembly. The Western
Allies want Bonn to accept. The
Germans have been hanging back
because they feel they are not
being invited to sit down as equals
with the other nations in what
amounts to an unofficial parlia-
ment of Western Europe.

BOSTON, Nov. 24.-Two sepa-

freezers.

morning. about 800 homes in the

days. Most Of the city and sew
eral suburban communities were
blacked out for an hour Sunday
night.

the Little Sisters of the Poor was
among the places left without heat
temporarily when the oil burner
was cut off.


A morning mass in st. Patrick's
Church on Dudley street was cele-
brated by candle light as the
electricity failed.


The police signal system was
cut of for while, but radio COM
munications were operating.

Comes early spring, all seeming
indifference is replaced by intense
interest in life. The egg yolk has
now been all absorbed and foraging
must take place. Smaller worms
and larvae piece out regular meals
The Salamander grows fast.


As time for transformation ap-
proaches, the larva gradually loses
his brownish color and takes on
the characteristics of his parents
The brownish color takes on a GRIM
son hue; the gills shrink to mere
stubs and disappear. The tail be-
comes more rounded as the keels
are absorbed. The teeth, lips and
tongue undergo change important
to the Salamander.


No one knows how long the young
salamander retains his brilliant
uniform. The older generation are
very dark red.


Adult salamanders in this tribe
reach length of six inches. They
are not socially inclined. They
feed readily in captivity. On their
own they are beset by many foes
In turn, the salamander enjoys in
sectS, small worms and such. They
are especially fond of earth worms
and they have been known to feast
on their own eggs. Their relatives
are very fond of them and know
where to find them.


These salamanders are autumn
prizes that can be kept over for
study purposes in school.

MARY O'GRADY


BY Mary LAWN. (Atlantic-Little

Mary LAWN, the gifted Amer
ican-born Irish writer, has had a
change of heart toward the
women of Ireland. Hitherto she
has painted them with ironic con-
tempt as nagging wives and pos
sessive mothers; now she presents
one who is the very personiflcation
of the maternal spirit, a great
hearted countrywoman whose
whole fulfillment has been in
bearing her children and in loving
them selflessly. The blacklist trag-
edies shadow Mary O'Grady's life.
Her little brood is scattered under
the most heartbreaking condi-
tions. Yet Mary accepts it all
with simple fortitude. piety and
many cups of tea.


Readers will look in vain here
for the tartness and telling shafts
which marked Miss LAWNS ear
lier work. She is all charity, all
sympathy for poor Mary O'Grady,
whose story she tells almost en-
tirely in dialogue, which relates
minutely, often monotonously, the
crises of domestic life. One can
commend, of course, the softening
of Miss LAWNS point of view.
while still bemoaning the lack of
bite and clarity which made her
short stories so memorable.


M, MEG,

WITH UNITED STATES 1st
CORPS, NORTH KOREA, Oct. %.
The bodies of 80 Americans have
been discovered in and near a
northbound train 80 miles north
east Of Anju.


Nine were badly burned. The
other 81 Americans had been shot.
Two survivors were found.


The judge advocate of the 1st
Corps said the northbound train
had been attacked and set afire
by American planes.


All Killed by Reds.


Information indicated that flee
ing Red Koreans had killed all
the Americans and nine of the
bodies later were burned in the
air strike. No Red Korean dead
were found.


South Koreans led M/Sergt.
Morgan L. Cochrane to the two
survivors and then to 20 bodies
alongside the track near Kujang
village.


The 3Oth was found later by
investigators.


Sergt. Cochrane filed today a
report on his discovery with the
judge advocate, Col. Merton F.
Ellis of San Francisco.


Sergt. Cochrane said: He was
on a reconnaissance mission last
Sunday when he was halted by
South Korean soldiers about 4
miles east of Kujang. The ROK
troops said they had found two
Americans.


2 Survivors Found.


Sergt. Cochrane followed the
South Koreans to a nearby hut
where he found two exhausted
GI's. They were so emaciated and
weak that they could only mutter
thanks for being rescued.


The South Koreans then said
they knew where there were
many. many" dead Americans.


They led him to the railroad
where he found 20 bodies laid out
on mats beside the still burning
train.


Nine burned bodies were in a
row beside the tracks. Twenty
others which had been shot were
nearby. Sergt. Cochrane buried
the bodies in three common
graves.


Sergt. Cochrane said the oead
Americans had not been bound
and that he saw no signs of tor
ture or mutilation.

AS you enter the salt marshes
where willets love to gather, you
are greeted with "pill-wil- -willet"
Every bird is alerted and joins in.


Most of the time the willets are
stationed in a favorite lookout-a
granite boulder. spruce tree or tele-
phone pole. When alone, they are
calm. Sportsmen dislike their sem
tinel habits, claiming that willets
warn better game.


Nothing is more beautiful that

wings, spread at full length, show
the pure white of the underwings
With the basal of the primaries and
the greater parts of the secondaries
lined with snowy white. Nearing
the earth they call "Will-et, will
will-et," in a tone drama of the salt
marsh, fortissimo warning to all
that trespassers have arrived. 1t
always amazes you to find how
long these birds can keep up their
calls without taking time out for
breath. But the moment you are out

Before landing, the long black
wings, white below, are brought to-
gether at the tips. Heads bowed thus
they remind you of pictures OF
archangels. -@


After this lovely gesture, the male
sings song of liquid. tender notes
which float out over the Jersey
marshes. His mate creeps along the
tunnel in the tall grass that leads
to her grass-lined nest wherein are
four pale brown eggs. She inspects
them carefully and looks eagerly
around, her head cooked first to one
side and then the other as she
listens to the endearing notes meant
only for her. Thus serenaded, she
settles down in the grassy cup to
keep her treasures warm.


The Western willet and Eastern
cousin differ much in size and color,
although habits and general appear
ance are Identical During their
autumn migration they visit sloughs
and marshes and try the patience
of sportsmen by loud cries that alert
more desirable birds.


Willets are distributed North and
South over our country. Nests are
found in Virginia and as far away as
Nova Scotia. Some are contented
with the Florida climate. Winters are
spent in belt from the Bahamas to
Brazil. They are rarely seen in
Bermuda and Europe.

drunk.


"I've never seen anything like
it." said one officer at the city
Jail drunk tank. They're stacked
up like cordwood."
| Many of the drunks will spend
Christmas in jail unless friends
or relatives can rescue them with

City police recorded 95 acci-

during the night shift last Near
Years eve only IS accidents were
reported.

On American planes flying over

old requirements to allow chlor-

inspection provisions of the pres
ent law and let any milk into the

ards set up by the Public Health

They may swallow their food with

contact like group in Jakarta,

RANGOON, Burma, Feb. 21.-
Three Burmese newspapers yes
terday called editorially for
prompt American aid to save
Burma from a Communist threat.
The three Rangoon English
language newspapers asked for
effective. demonstrable proof that
American friendship for Burma
does not exist solely for what the
United States can get from this
country.


The Burman asserted that the
menace from Communist China
has become a close reality.


Two Armed Groups Mentioned.


Stating that there exists in
Burma two armed Communist
groups. the Burman said these
groups would not hesitate to
make the country Communist.
Another paper, the independent,
Nation, expressed fear of forced
entry of communism into Burma.
1t said the general feeling of Bur-
mese is that the Western democ-
racies have abandoned Burma to
any possible fate.


The Nation criticized American
politicians for "studiously contin-
uing to ignore Burma" thereby
allowing unchecked Communist
propaganda.


Change in Policy Urged.


The paper expressed the hope
that America soon would re-
orient its policy in the realization
that it was better possibly to lose
few million dollars in helping
Burma through this period than
drive her to desperation by re
naming piously aloof."
The influential weekly, Monday
New Times and Burmese Review
said troubled Burma remains a
danger to Southeast Asias stabil-
ity. No one can be complacent,
the paper said, until Burma is back
on her feet.

ware and Pennsylvania. After long litigation,
the British courts had suggested that it was
desirable for specific lines to be run separating
the three colonies. Local surveyors did the
work along the Maryland-Delaware border.
Charles Mason and jeremiah Dixon checked
their findings and then pushed out to the West.


Their going was tough. During four years
they made only about 230 miles, setting up
markers OF limestone proceSSed in England.
Those stakes" carried the arms OF the Calvert
and Penn families and were meant to survive
the wear and tear OF centuries. But there also
were smaller stones, inscribed simply with
initials, placed at five-mile intervals The task
of installing the markers was relatively tedious
one, but the job of running the line was much
more difficult. Mason and Dixon had to fight
the weather and to avoid fighting the Indians.
They passed over mountains, through deep
valleys, across rivers. through dense forests.
Much hardship was involved in their enterprise.
But they were successful. Such errors as they
failed to correct were minor. They came to the
end Of their effort at Sideling Hill in what now
is Washington County, Pennsylvania. Indians
halted their further progress, and they returned
East with the knowledge that, even so, they had
established border which practically "lieth
under the 10th degree of north latitude from
the equinoctial." It was not until the debates
on Congress leading to the Missouri Compromise
in 1920 that the Mason-Dixon Line was con-
sidered to divide the North and the South, the
free States and the slave.


Meanwhile, the two British surveyors dis
appeared from history. Mason is believed to
have died in 1887. What happened to Dixon is
question for which there is no answer in
available reference books.

Scarcity of eggs in this area
kept retail prices unchanged or
sent them slightly higher in
Washington stores today, despite
a dip of from 2 to 6 cents dozen
in some other sections of the East.


Large grade A eggs sold at
about 80 cents a dozen in one
large retail chain group here,
about 2 cents above last weeks
listing. Dealers explained, how
ever, that there has been no gen.
eral increase since last week when
some egg prices rose as much as
10 cents a dozen.


Agriculture Department experts
said the egg supply should be
more plentiful in December.


Pork Shows Decline.

that showed any appreciable
change in retail prices here this
week. One chain organization re-
ported drops between 6 and 10
cents on some center chops and
whole loin roasts but noted that
those reductions did not reflect
any such trend in the pork mar
ket generally.


Recent storms and low tenn

wove baskets to carry water, and
began packing clay inside to keep
the baskets from leaking. The
people noticed how the clay would
harden and form a waterproof

After Cortez conquered Mexico

immigration authorities an
nounced both men will be held in
Winchester jail until August 80,

aboard the Batory on her return
trip to New York.


The two are William Jesse New
ton, 26, of New York and Howard
Campbell, 29-year-old Stowaway
of Des MoineS, Iowa.


Newton was taken aboard in
the Atlantic Ocean about 100
miles off New York after he landed
his rented seaplane alongside the
ship August 8.


Gas Supply Was Gone.


Capt. Jan CwiklinSki said the
flyer told him he lost his way
and was almost out of gasoline.
There was not quite half-a-
gallon of gasoline in the planes
tank" the captain said.


Campbell came down the ships
gangway quietly, but Newton pro-
tested volubly as he was put into
the police van.


They were taken into custody
by Detective Supt. Gordon Baker
of the Southampton police and
Detective Sergt. Bill Bentley of
Scotland Yard.


Charge Is Not Revealed.


Sergt. Bentley was one of the
Scotland Yard men who arrested
Communist Gerhard Eisler when
he arrived here in the same ship
on his fight from the United
States in May, 1949. Eisler later
was released by a British court
and continued his journey to East
Germany.


Campbell, as a Stowaway, prob
ably will be detained here pending
return to the United States
A United States consular at
tache accompanied the police off,
GERS aboard the Batory and went
with them and their two prison.
ers to police headquarters.
The exact charge against the
two Americans was not revealed.

HONG KONG. July Red
China's chairman Mao Tze-tung
yesterday signed the agrarian re-
form law.


Published here by the official
New China News agency, the
8,000-word text makes startling
concessions to China's land capi-
talists and rich peasants.


Landlords in Central and South
China are due to have their land
holdings. farm implements and
surplus houses" confiscated, but
will be allowed to retain other
wealth under the law. Rich peas
ants who till their own land and
hire other peasants will be allowed
to keep all their wealth and land
as before.


These concessions contrast with
the harsh policy in Manchuria
where landlords were stripped of
all wealth and driven from their
homes, and where rich peasants
were stripped to the level of ordi-
nary peasants.

The Atlas Club has been an

action to dissolve the charter of

a drive against after-hours bottle

abusing their charters, which in
most cases spelled out charitable
aims alone. The dissolution suit
was dropped when the Atlas man
agement gave assurances the club
would cease after-hours liquor

license.

activities yesterday. He declared
that six years ago $4,000 was con-
tributed to Children's Hospital and
that other sizable sums were given
to the Children's Receiving Home,
the Red Cross and the Community
Chest here.

showing such gifts are incomplete,
owing to careless former secre-
tary and because the Internal
Revenue Bureau still has certain
club papers in its possession to de-
ternlne whether Atlas owes the
Government cabaret taxes.

ing offer.

CHICAGO, Jan. 28.-One wom-
an was killed and eight other per-
sons were injured, some believed
seriously, early today when fire
swept through a three-story North
Side rooming house.


Several persons leaped from
windows as flames whipped
through the brick fiat building at
2l42 North Clark street. Firemen
said at least four suffered injuries
after leaping and were hospital
lied. Others hospitalized were
overcome by smoke. Some so per-
sons fled in their night clothes
from the burning structure.


Mrs. Helen Ford, So, died in
the lobby of a nearby hotel after
firemen removed her and her
daughter. Sandra Lee, from their
apartment. Both were overcome
by smoke.


The cause of the fire was not
determined.

One, Injuries 8 in CHICAGO

An Associated Press story from Cochran
Georgia, Monday filled only three inches Of
one column of space in The Star, but many who
read it will remember it long after supposedly
more important matters have been forgotten
1t told how man and his wife were on their
way to hospital with their infant daughter
when their car broke down. The parents vainly
tried to persuade other travellers to give them
lift. But nobody stopped-that is, nobody
stopped until unidentified colored man came
along, saw their signals and pulled up by the
side of the road and took them in. With his
help, the distressed little family finally reached
the hospital


The story ended on tragic note. Doctors
pronounced the baby dead on arrival. The child
had pneumonia and might not have survived
the trip even If there had been no delay But
her parents are not any the less grateful to their
unknown friend. He passes into history simply
as another anonymous Good Samaritan, neigh
Dor when neighborliness was needed.
headline: A Modern Good Samaritan

text:
The North American Radio
Conference ended last night with
an agreement which delegates
said will mean better radio recep-
tion for many areas in the United
States and Cuba.


The agreement fixes regional
use OF channels by the United
States, Cuba, Canada, the Ba-
hamas, Jamaica and the Domint-
can Republic.


Mexico originally participated
IN the conference but Withdrew
several weeks ago when its dele
gates decided they could not reach
settlement with other members,
particularly the United States.


The compromise between the
United States and Cuba was
hailed by officials as a major
achievement Cuba walked out
of Montreal conference last year
when it could not agree with the
United States on assignment of
radio frequencies in the North
American region.


There was little or no disagree
ment between other areas.


One official said the new agree
ment means both Cuba and the
United States will have better
reception on a wider range of
radio frequencies.


Cuba repeatedly won its battle
for use of an additional number
of channels, it was said. These
channels will be shared with
United States stations, but will
not interfere with reception in
either country.
headline:
North American Radio
Agreement Reached

NEW YORK, Nov. 25.-The Nor
wegian American Line motorship
Lungenfjord caught fire off storm
swept Long Island today, but re-
ported later the blaze was under
control.


The Coast Guard said at 6:45
pm. tEST) that the ship reported
it was proceeding to New York
under its own power.


The ships SOS was received at
5 pm. (EST), the Coast Guard
said. Her position was given as
"just south of Shinnecock Bay"
which is off the summer resort of
Southampton, 80 miles from New
York City.


The Coast Guard cutter Yeaton
was sent to aid the ship.


The freighter Steelworker, which
was near the scene, said it also
was answering the Lyngenfjord's s
call for help.

Catches Fire in Storm

ously from afternoon to past mid

surrounding area poured into the
monastery churches, indicating
that Russia has many believers.
though some of the interest was
curiosity.

In Russian Orthodox Church

Korean Ambassador John M
Chang estimated yesterday that
easily 10 million refugees in his
country will need help to live
through the forthcoming winter


The Ambassador made the
statement after talking for As min
uteS with Assistant Secretary of
State Dean RuSk about assistance
to the refugees.


The Ambassador said the prob
lem of co-ordinating relief for Ko-
rea has been solved but the main
problem of transporting supplies
from Japan, the United States
and elsewhere remains to be
worked out.


Noting that Korean winters are
very severe, the Ambassador
pointed out that farmers had been
unable to gather their crops and
that the refugees have few per-
sonal effects with them.


The Ambassador said some
American relief supplies such as
clothing, foodstuffs and medicines
already have arrived from Japan.

Korean Envoy Seeks Help
For 10 Million Refugees

patches.

Greater love hath no man than
this, that man lay down his life
for his friends"


These words from the Scriptures
had great meaning for President
Truman yesterday, for they were
spoken of a man who died in his
behalf.


Oscar Coffelt had sacrificed his
life that Mr.. Truman might live.
The 40-year-old White House
policeman fell, mortally wounded,
in the shower of bullets in front
Of Blair House last Wednesday.


Mr.. and Mrs. Truman sat at
the front of Fort Myer Chapel yes
terday during the services for Pvt.
Coffelt.


Near them was the flag -draped
casket of the policeman, and not
far away were Mrs. Coffelt and
the mother of the man who died
defending the President.


Outside, the United States Army
band played Nearer, My God, to
Thee" in the solemn tones which
marked it's performance through
out the ceremony.


Unusual Security Guard.


Mr.. and Mrs. Truman were
taken to Arlington Cemetery
under security measures seldom
equalled for a President.


Around Blair House. their tenn
porary home, police stood guard
behind a roped-off sidewalk until
the motorcade pushed off shortly
before II am.


Ahead of the presidential party
had gone other elements of the
funeral, including the body headed
by more than SO motorcycle po-
licemen.


Before the chapel scores of other
policemen stood in formation,
squads of Metropolitan and Park
police. In the area, and along
the route. soldiers with bayonets
guarded the President.


Dean John w. Suter of the
Washington Cathedral and 1t. Col.
Robert M. Homiston, Fort Myer
chaplain. spoke prayers for the
deceased and for Mr.. Truman.


At the conclusion of the service
the casket was wheeled out. Mr..
and Mrs. Truman followed. their
faces expressing profound sadness.


Moving Ceremony.


The cavalcade moved through
the autumnal atmosphere of vari-
colored leaves, tombStoneS OF
many hero marking the way.


The band played, quietly, feel
ingly. 1t played familiar hymns
until the grave was reached and
the family of the policeman, a
World War II veteran. formed
under the graves canopy.


There, too, were Mr.. and Mrs.
Truman, standing during the COM
initial services, and while Masons
added their rites.


A firing party honored Mr.. Cof-
felt with three voleys. Then there
were taps-close at hand, and with
q distant echo.


In the intense stiffness there
after, Mr.. and Mrs. Truman moved
to their car. The President had
honored hero.

second and third.

SAN FRANCISCO, Dec. 12.-
The Coast Guard said last night
that tugboat and a Government
tanker it was towing came close
to disaster when they scraped
across the sunken Navy hospital
ship Benevolence outside the
Golden Gate.


Statements of the men aboard
the ships raised the possibility
that the Benevolence, sunk in a
collision with the Mary Lucken-
bach on August 25, may have
broken loose from a shoal on
which she lay to become floating
derelict.


Involved in the accident were
the Red Stack tug Relief and the
Neches, military Sea Transport
Service tanker being towed here
from San Diego for reconditioning.
The Relief had an 8-foot section
of her keel knocked off. The
Neches had dents, holes and
scrapes all along her keel.
headline:

PeriIs Tug and Tanker

LONDON, Feb. 24.-Thousand.
of rain-soaked Londoners jam
med Piccadilly Circus and nearby
Trafalgar Square until the early
morning hours today to cheer OF
jeer the election results.


The atmosphere was that OF
New Years eve, enlivened by
bursts Of fireworks, as electric il
Illuminated boards flashed the re-
turns.


Conservative victories were sig
nailed by a sea of balloons, union
jacks and blue and white stars
Labor successes got an answering
wave of red and yellow balloons


Flower girls and hawkers of bal
looms and noise makers did a land
Office business in Piccadilly. Some
pranksters improvised their noise
makers by touching balloons with
lighted cigarettes.


British pubs, unlike bars in most
American States. remained open
during the election. They did not
close until midnight. Clubs and
restaurants got permission to serve
patrons into the wee hours.


AS Labor zoomed into the lead
the expensive night spots dis
pensed mainly liquid cheer. The
crowds, chiefly pro-Labor, grew
more enthusiastic by the hour.


Stay Until After Dawn


The merrymakers found the
proceedings so enjoyable that the
last stragglers didn't desert Gen.
tral London until after dawn.


Labor Party headquarters was
quietly confident. Tory head
quarters staged early celebrations
as Conservative candidates piled
up local victories, but gathering
gloom set in as the Laborites
forged ahead. Hope came back to
life later.


Most of the Tory leaders were
at Winston Churchill's Hyde Park
home, where the results came in
by teletype.


The Liberals. who may be fin
ished as an effective force by
their crushing defeat, were the
quietest of all.


King George vi got the elec-
ton returns as millions of his sub
jects did-by radio and television


Princess Elizabeth drove from
her home, Clarence House, and
joined the King, Queen Elizabeth
and Princess Margaret at Buck
ingham Palace. They dined to-
gether while waiting for the Brit
ish Broadcasting Corp. to report
the first results.


King Can't Vote.


The British constitution bars
the King from voting. Other
members Of the royal family ira
ditionally stay away from the
polls, too.


After the final result is known,
the King will summon the leader
OF the winning party and ask him
to form a new government.


Mr.. Attlee glad-handed the
voters yesterday. took a three
hour nap and then got together
with his old friends and fellow
cabinet ministers last night to

NEW YORK, July 22.-The
possibility the Korean war will
bring additional military orders
for cotton goods stimulated buy
ing interest in the cotton textile
market this week despite higher
prices.


Little actual business was trans
acted, however, with leading mills
sitting on the Sidelines until raw
cotton prices stabilize.


President Truman's request for
$40 billion in additional military
spending was expected to expand
the demand for cotton.


But most observers said there
was no justification for any fears
of a textile shortage, excepting
where speculation is involved.


Many mills have withdrawn
from the market during the past
couple of weeks to reprice their
goods and bring them more in
line with increased raw material
costs.


There was little yardage avail
able in the popular print cloths
and broadclothS for the balance
of the year and sales were scat
tered. The popular 80-square
print cloth moved up to 241a
cents yard.

The ice storm which fattened
communications and power lines
over a wide section of the Upper
Midwest yesterday had shrunk to
the Northern Great Lakes region
today.


Northeastern Iowa generally
and the Mississippi River city of
Clinton particularly, were hardest
hit by the freezing rain which
disabled telephone service in at
least SIS towns of the area.


Mayor Don Allison of Clinton
estimated the icestorm caused 81
million damage there.


But rising temperatures in all
but the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wis
consin and Michigan today gave
many Of the stricken communi-
ties a chance to repair the dam
age.


Rain continued falling over
much of Eastern Iowa, however.


Phone Lines Down.


Damage was estimated at more
than 100000 to the telephone
systems of Iowa alone. The freez-
ing rain there ripped down lines
faster than emergency repairs
could be made and many families
shivered in their homes because
of power failure. Electrically
powered furnace stokers were dis
abled and some families depend
ent on electricity for cooking pur-
poses had to forego Easter meals.


One of first tasks for telephone
crewmen at Clinton was TO restore
connections between the town and
the outside world. and to get
more than 500 telephones back
into service.


To provide a quick link between
Clinton and Davenport for emerg-
ency calls, Northwestern Bell
Telephone Co. set up a radio tele-
phone unit.


Meanwhile. ham" radio oper-
ators who throughout the night
maintained contact with amateur
operators in other cities, con-
tinued on the job.


They handled all messages for
the three railroads that operate
into Clinton-the Rock Island,
Milwaukee and the Chicago &
North Western.


The storms are extended gen.
orally from Northern Indiana and
Illinois westward through most
of Iowa and northward through
the Great Lakes region.


While the temperatures at Des
MoineS lowered only a few de-
grees above freezing during the
storm, the mercury at Lincoln,
Nebr., only $50 miles to the west,
climbed to high Of 81 degrees.


Heavy snow was reported falling
today at Rapid City, S. Dak.. with
continued freezing rain in North
ern Minnesota and Northern Wis
Consin. The storm was moving
eastward and was expected to hit
Upper Michigan today.


More Duststorms.


Elsewhere over the Nation, skies
generally were clear and tempera-
lures near or above seasonal levels.


Another duststorm was the
Easter weather fare over some
areas of Western Kansas, the
Texas Panhandle and Eastern New
Mexico. Winds up to 56 miles
an hour were so laden with soil
at Dalhart, Tex, that visibility at
times was reduced to miles.


Residents at Rock Falls and
Sterling, ILL.,, were warned to stay
of the streets yesterday because
of danger from power lines that
had been ripped down by the
heavy ice coating. The towns Of
Princeton and Ohio were reported
cut off from outside communica-
ton while Morris and Mendoza
reported their cities had to use
candles or kerosene lamps for
Easter church service lighting.

Bees make combs from wax. Some
of these are used for storing honey,
but others are the places where
young bees grow up. Inside the cell,
there is a change from egg to grub,
and then to bee.


Three kinds of cells are made.
The smallest are only about one fifth
of an inch wide, and are used for
eggs which will produce worker bees.
Slightly larger are the cells for
drones, and largest of all are those
for queen bees.


Before the Matching, there is one
queen in the hive. She never goes
out to gather honey; she stays home
to lay eggs. In single day she
may lay 1000 or 5000 eggs.


Worker bees feed the queen. Her
needs are taken care of by a dozen
or more workers, and they guard her
all the time.


The workers have stings, or sting
erS, which are barbed. When they
sting, they usually lose their stingers
and die.


The queen also has stinger. but
it, is smooth around the edges.
This stinger can be used over and
over again without harm to the
queen.


The queen bee has Jealous
nature. She lays eggs which will
turn into new queens, but she grows
jealous of the young ones.


Several new queens may develop
in brood. The old queen edges
toward their cells, and would like
to sting them to death. Workers
crowd around her, however, and |
keep her away from the young
queens so far as possible.


only one queen to hive" may
be called the rule among honey
bees, and we ask, What happens
when young queens are produced?"


One of the young queens may
rule the old hive The rest are
slain, or take away swarms. If a.
new ruler comes to the old hive the
old queen takes a swarm away.

THE South Korean Army-widely re-


L ported to have been destroyed in the
first week of the war-today is paying
back the North Koreans for eafly defeats
in some of the bitterest fighting Of this
savage campaign.


About 10000 "ROK" troops have scored
one success after another against an
enemy which is still superior in numbers
and arms. Fighting almost without rest,
they have used every possible tactical de-
vice to counterattack the Communists
while fulfilling their primary mission of
holding the Pusan perimeter at the side
OF American soldiers and Marines.


Their greatest asset to the American
command is their reliability and dis
cipline. One American staff officer, ad-
mitting he had underestimate the South
Korean troops at first, paid them the
highest compliment in the book: "They
go where you tell them and they stay
there until you tell them to pull back"
This tenacity has been tested by assign
ing Korean troops to cover retreats of the
main forces on several occasions.


Where every man or gun makes diff
ference, the South Korean forces have
been vital in helping to keep the Red in
vaders from throwing the Allied forces
into the sea. But recognition has been
slow in coming, and the bitter defeats of
the first few days of the war are still
remembered by the American public.


After heroic but hopeless stand at
the gates of Seoul for more than day,
the South Korean forces snapped under
the pressure OF enemy armor, air power,
heavy artillery and massed infantry.
Soldiers were reported to have refused to
mine roads, discarded their weapons and
fed to the hills. Others retreated in dis
order.


There was rash criticism of the train
ing and courage of the ROK troops.
It was suggested that the average soldier
would not fight for the corrupt Rhee
regime" But when American troops
met the North Koreans in combat, the
truth became evident. The enemy had
been underestimated; he had artillery
which outranged ours, his tanks were
impervious to our AT weapons and his
troops were combat-Seasoned.


Now the South Korean Army has

French bombers virtually wiped

be dead. There have been re-

air attack.

Twelve days after he felt the

What a scene was there for him
to see! All the houses in Concep-

The earthquake had caused many
shocks, but the worst one had come
just before noon. The people had
rushed out of their houses, and
most of them had escaped with
their lives.


Following the quaking Of the
earth, huge waves had rushed In
from the ocean and had swept
through the streets. Falling back,
the water had carried all manner
of objects-chairs, tables, beds and
so Onto the coast. Scores of per-
sons died, but the loss of life was
less than If the houses had beer,
shaken down at night.


Natives of the area told Darwin
that the bottom of the sea had
risen. This interested him q great
deal. Near an island 80 miles from
the coast, there were rocks with
mussel shells clinging to them at
places 10 feet above the high-water
mark. In past times men had diyed
for mussels at the spot. and it was
plain that the rocks had been raised
20 or 80 feet.


The Beagle kept sailing north
ward. Parts of Northern Chile and
Southern Peru were visited. During
this part OF his journey, Darwin
learned something about the an
cient Incas, and saw famous
bridge which had served the Incas
hundreds of years before.


Leaving Peru, the Beagle" made
its way to the Galapagos Islands.
Onrthese islands Darwin gave special
study. to. the large lizards and
turtles which he found there.

his innocence.
